=== page 7 ===
India’s growth story is being built in steel, infrastructure, energy 
transition assets and industrial capacity. At the heart of that story 
is iron ore: a mineral that does not merely feed furnaces, but 
enables roads, railways, ports, cities, manufacturing and national 
resilience.
In FY 2025-26, NMDC crossed a defining threshold, producing 53 
million tonnes of iron ore and reinforcing its role as India’s largest 
iron ore producer. This achievement reflects more than scale. It 
reflects the strength of an integrated mining system: ore body 
knowledge, safe operations, processing capability, evacuation 
infrastructure, customer responsiveness and disciplined execution 
working together.
“Powering the Nation. Sustaining the Future.” captures this dual 
responsibility. NMDC is powering the nation by securing the raw 
material base for India’s steel-led development. It is sustaining the 
future by expanding with responsibility: investing in technology, 
improving operational efficiency, strengthening logistics, 
deepening environmental stewardship and preparing for a lower-
impact, more resilient mining model.
As NMDC advances towards its long-term capacity ambition, the 
measure of progress will be broader than volume alone. It will 
be the Company’s ability to deliver reliable supply, disciplined 
growth, safer operations and responsible value creation. That is 
the promise of this year’s theme: building the materials of national 
progress while protecting the foundations of tomorrow.

Dear Stakeholders,
It gives me immense pleasure to present the Annual Report of NMDC Limited for FY 
2025-26, a year marked by strong performance, significant milestones and continued 
progress towards our long-term vision.
The year 2026 has marked an important chapter in our national journey. Despite 
global economic and geopolitical uncertainties, India’s progress remains steady and 
decisive. Our real GDP growth of 7.7% in FY26 reflects the strength of our economy and 
investment momentum. India is also asserting leadership in technology, innovation and 
global partnerships.
For NMDC, this has been a year  replete with ‘Eureka’ moments where we discovered 
and rediscovered our true calling and embarked on a journey of  profound transformation 
to harness  our real potential. In FY26, we became the first mining company in India 
to produce more than 50 million tonnes of iron ore in a single year, achieving record 
production of 53.16 million tonnes and sales of 50.24 million tonnes, scripting history 
on stone. The numbers reflect an increase of 20.62% in production and 13.15% in sales 
year on year, which have been achieved organically, by optimizing and exceeding 
the capacities and capabilities of the existing production and sales equipments and 
infrastructure. NMDC has proved its resilience with such a quantum jump in production 
in a single year which is unprecedented and unparalleled in the industry. Through this 
commendable performance, NMDC has genuinely contributed to the strengthening of 
the foundation for India’s infrastructure and industrial growth.
This operational excellence was naturally reflected in the financial performance of the 
Company which registered  new  echelons in turnover and other financial parameters.. 
Revenue from operations increased by 33.31% to `31,554 crore, Profit After Tax rose 
by 10.88% to `7,421 crore and Net Worth increased by 14.39% to `33,836 crore. NMDC 
invested `3,384 crore in capital expenditure during the year while continuing to create 
value for shareholders through a proposed total dividend of `3.50 per share for FY 2025-
26, subject to shareholders’ approval.
India’s rapid industrialisation calls for secure, reliable and responsibly managed mineral 
resources. Our Vision 2030 of achieving 100 MTPA of iron ore production capacity is 
therefore not merely a business ambition, but an important contribution towards India’s 
long-term mineral security and economic growth. 
Strengthening the Growth Platform
The next phase of NMDC’s journey is focused on converting capacity and ambition into 
safe, efficient and dependable operations. Our 60 MT production target for FY 2026-27 
represents an important step towards the 100 MTPA pathway.
Significant progress was achieved in strengthening our integrated mining and logistics 
infrastructure. The Kirandul–Jagdalpur rail-line doubling project achieved 97% overall 
progress, with 128 km completed and operational, while the slurry pipeline project

reached 94% progress as on 31st March 2026. Along with associated processing and 
pelletisation facilities, these projects will enhance evacuation capacity and improve the 
overall efficiency of the Bailadila value chain. Going forward, we expect to see these 
important projects getting commissioned and reinforcing the Company’s efforts in 
becoming a marquee player in the green steel value chain. 
NMDC also continued to diversify its domestic mineral portfolio. Tokisud North in 
Jharkhand commenced mining operations in January 2026, marking our entry into 
domestic coal mining. The groundbreaking of Bailadila Iron Ore Deposit-4, through 
NMDC-CMDC Limited, was undertaken in February 2026, with efforts underway towards 
commencement of commercial operations. Significant progress  in the development 
of Bailadila Iron Ore Deposit-13, which is also a part of NMDC-CMDC Limited, were 
undertaken during FY 2025-26, leading to its commissioning in the months that 
followed. 
It also makes me proud to inform that NMDC, in true recognition of the tireless and 
dedicated efforts of its human capital, made concerted efforts to provide quality life 
to its employees in the projects by commissioning new housing and anciliary facilities 
during the year and also undertaking the commencement of a few other such projects in 
its townships at Bailadila and Donimalai complexes.
Our earnestness and seriousness to emerge as a world class, global mineral behemoth 
took a significant leap with the opening of our offices in  Dubai, UAE and Sydney, 
Australia. These offices are expected to support in NMDC’s mineral diversification 
journey abroad. 
Technology, Sustainability and People
State of Art Technology and innovation are an integral part of NMDC’s operations with 
an objective to improving operational visibility, decision-making, productivity and safety. 
Initiatives taken up include Digital Project Management Unit, Automated Sampling, 
Digitally Enabled Drilling and Blasting, Real-Time Material Visibility and Integrated 
Sustainability Data Systems. 
Our commitment to responsible growth remains equally strong. NMDC is pursuing 
greater energy and resource efficiency, increased renewable energy utilisation, improved 
water and land stewardship and lower-carbon logistics. Our Net Zero Strategy and 
Roadmap provides a structured direction for reducing the environmental footprint of our 
operations.
Our people remain at the heart of this transformation. Safety continues to be a non-
negotiable priority, complemented by focused investments in human capital through 
skill development, leadership enhancement and digital capabilities. Through our 
CSR initiatives, NMDC also continues to contribute to healthcare, education, skill 
development and community infrastructure, particularly in the regions surrounding our 
operations.

Corporate Governance
Corporate governance remains a cornerstone of NMDC’s organisational ethos, 
underpinning every aspect of our operations and decision-making. We are committed 
to creating sustainable long-term value for all our stakeholders including shareholders, 
customers, suppliers, creditors, the Government of India, State Governments, regulatory 
authorities, and the communities we serve. Guided by the highest standards of 
integrity and accountability, we strive to ensure full compliance with applicable laws 
and regulations, both in letter and spirit. Through transparent governance practices, 
prudent risk management and responsible decision-making, we continue to strengthen 
stakeholder confidence and safeguard value creation.
Looking Ahead
The year ahead will be the year of   execution, consolidation and transformation. 
Stabilising our higher production base, reaching the 60 MT production milestone, 
completing critical infrastructure projects and advancing the next phases of capacity 
expansion will remain key priorities.
The journey towards 100 MTPA will require operational excellence, disciplined capital 
allocation, strong project execution, technology adoption and unwavering commitment 
to safety and sustainability. At the same time, NMDC will continue to explore 
opportunities for diversification into critical and strategic minerals, both domestically 
and internationally, in alignment with India’s evolving mineral security needs.
I am confident that NMDC has the resources, capabilities and institutional strength to 
meet the opportunities and challenges ahead. We are building an enterprise that is 
larger in scale, stronger in capability, smarter through technology and more responsible 
in its operations.
I express my sincere gratitude to the Government of India, Ministry of Steel, Ministry 
of Mines, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, other Government 
Departments and the State Governments for their continued guidance and support.
I also thank our employees and their unions, customers, suppliers, partners, host 
communities, regulators and shareholders for their continued trust and confidence.
Together, we will continue to build NMDC as a globally competitive mining enterprise 
and remain at the heart of India’s journey towards a stronger, more self-reliant and 
mineral-secure future.
Jai Hind!
Amitava Mukherjee
Chairman & Managing Director

NMDC's FY 2025-26 Integrated Annual Report is organised around the way the enterprise creates value. It begins with the year's 
defining outcomes and the context in which NMDC operates. It then moves through strategic direction and the business model, 
examines how value moves through the six capitals, and brings together ESG, climate, risk, governance, statutory and financial 
reporting. This structure enables readers to connect a management decision with the resources it uses, the operating result it 
produces, the stakeholder outcome it influences and the risk or trade-off that must be governed.

FIVE-YEAR PERFORMANCE SNAPSHOT
The five-year performance trajectory of 
NMDC Limited for the period concluding 
31st March 2026 provides empirical 
evidence of an enterprise in the midst of 
a historic transformation. This snapshot 
does not merely record financial and 
physical metrics; it narrates the story 
of how India’s premier Navratna mining enterprise has successfully transitioned from around 34 million tonne (MT) in financial 
year 2020-21 to breaching the monumental 50 million tonne production threshold and 
finishing with 53+ MT in the current fiscal year. This momentum serves as the definitive 
operational foundation for our “Vision 2030,” which aims to double our current capacity 
to 100 million tonnes per annum to safeguard the resource security of a Viksit Bharat. 
By maintaining a disciplined focus on volume-led growth and cost-competitiveness—
operating at one of the lowest cash costs globally—we have ensured that our financial 
performance remains resilient against the cyclical volatilities of the global iron ore 
market.THE 100 MILLION TONNE MOMENTUM:

The physical output of NMDC over the last 
five years demonstrates an impressive 
growth profile. Having achieved 45.02 
million tonnes in financial year 2023-24, 
we experienced a minor consolidation 
in financial year 2024-25 before surging 
to record-breaking levels in the first nine months of the current year. Our production reached 42.65 million tonnes by January 
2026, representing a 19% year-on-year increase and paving the clear operational runway 
to cross the 50 million tonne annual threshold for the first time in our seven-decade 
history. This scale-up is further bolstered by the historic operationalisation of the Coal 
Division in Jharkhand diversifying our manufactured capital and enhancing our role as a 
multi-mineral powerhouse.PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE: BREACHING THE 50 
MILLION TONNE THRESHOLD

capital expansion. From a turnover of 
approximately Indian Rupees 15,370 crore 
in financial year 2020-21, our revenue 
The strength of our balance sheet is best exemplified by our rising 
Net Worth, which has grown from Indian Rupees 17,875 crore in 
financial year 2021-22, the first full year following the demerger 
of the steel unit, to Indian Rupees 33,836 crore in financial year 
2025-26 — an expansion of close to 89%, at a compound annual 
growth rate of 17.3%. Built almost entirely from internal accruals on a from operations has more than doubled to Indian Rupees 31,554 crore in financial year 
2025-26, a compound annual growth of roughly 15.5% and a 33.31% increase over 
the Indian Rupees 23,668 crore recorded in financial year 2024-25. Profit After Tax 
rose to Indian Rupees 7,421 crore in financial year 2025-26, a growth of 10.88%, with 
EBITDA strengthening to Indian Rupees 10,737 crore on the back of record production 
of 53.16 million tonnes and sales of 50.24 million tonnes. Net worth has expanded to 
Indian Rupees 33,836 crore and earnings per share to Indian Rupees 8.44, supporting 
a dividend of Indian Rupees 3.50 per share while sustaining an ambitious Capital 
Expenditure (CAPEX) roadmap towards 2030.

At NMDC Limited, our identity is forged 
not only by the minerals we extract but 
by the purpose we uphold - to mine 
with meaning. As a premier “Navratna” 
Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) 
under the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Steel, Government of India, 
we stand at the intersection of industrial 
growth, national service, and responsible 
mining.   For over six decades, NMDC 
has been the primary guarantor of 
India’s mineral wealth, evolving from a 
single-mineral giant into a technology-
led, multi-mineral powerhouse. In the 
financial year concluding 31st March 2026, 
we have reached a historic inflection 
point: breaching the 50 million tonne 
(MT) annual production threshold. This 
milestone is not merely a quantitative OUR COMPASS POINTS NORTH  -  
toward innovation, sustainability, and a 100 million 
tonnes strong future.
achievement; it is the foundational 
momentum required to double our 
capacity to 100 million tonnes by 2030, 
securing the resource sovereignty of a 
Viksit Bharat.
Our Core Identity and  
National Mandate
Founded on 15th November 1958, NMDC 
is India’s largest iron ore producer and is 
globally recognized as one of the world’s 
lowest-cost producers.   We operate 
highly mechanized mines in Chhattisgarh 
and Karnataka, alongside India’s only 
mechanized diamond mine in Panna, 
Madhya Pradesh.  Our mandate extends 
beyond extraction; we are nation-builders 
dedicated to transforming the societies 
in which we operate while maintaining a “sacred harmony with nature”.   In 
FY2026, we formally operationalized our 
Coal Division, signifying our successful 
diversification into domestic coal mining to 
support India’s energy future. 
NMDC 2.0: Mining the Future
The transition into “NMDC 2.0” represents 
our manifestation of a future-ready 
enterprise that integrates “Smart Mining” 
with global ESG leadership.  By digitizing 
our core through Project Kalpataru (SAP 
S/4 HANA) and utilizing our UNIDO-
recognized R&D Centre, we are pioneering 
“Decision Intelligence” across our value 
chain.   This transformation ensures that 
our growth is scientific, sustainable, 
and capable of delivering value in an 
increasingly ESG-focused global economy.

SUSTAINABLE SCALE: HARMONISING  
50 MT PRODUCTION WITH ECOLOGICAL 
RESTORATION
NMDC Limited acknowledges that scaling production 
to exceed 50 million tonnes annually requires a 
sophisticated management of the “Natural Capital 
trade-off,” wherein the necessity of mineral extraction 
is systematically balanced against the imperative 
of ecosystem restoration. This equilibrium is most 
prominently maintained at the Panna Diamond Mining 
Project - the only Category “A” mine in India permitted 
by the Honourable Supreme Court to operate within 
an eco-sensitive zone - where the company has 
institutionalised rigorous safeguards, including the construction of a 30-lakh cubic metre reservoir to support 
watershed rejuvenation and the local flora and fauna. By scaling 
afforestation efforts to over 3.0 million trees since inception 
and adhering to site-specific Biodiversity Management Plans, 
the enterprise effectively decouples its industrial growth from 
environmental degradation. Furthermore, the integration 
of advanced Zero Liquid Discharge systems and real-time 
environmental monitoring across all complexes ensures that 
NMDC’s expansion remains harmonious with nature, fulfilling 
its strategic mandate as a responsible custodian of national 
resources.

GLOBAL CORRIDORS AND STRATEGIC DIVERSIFICATIONThe bedrock of our manufactured 
capital remains our highly mechanized 
mining complexes in Chhattisgarh

the current fiscal year marks the historic 
operationalization of our Coal Division 
in Jharkhand. NMDC has appointed 
MDO for Tokisud North Coal Block where 
operations have started from January 
2026. Operations at Rohne Coal block is 
expected to start soon.
NMDC’s footprint now extends far beyond 
the Indian subcontinent, reflecting our 
ambition to become a global mining 
major. Through our Australian subsidiary, 
Legacy Iron Ore Limited, we have 
successfully moved from exploration 
to production at the Mount Celia Gold Project while aggressively pursuing lithium-bearing pegmatites to support India’s green 
energy transition. In Mozambique, our 26% stake in International Coal Ventures Private 
Limited (ICVL) ensures a steady supply of coking coal from the Benga mine, safeguarding 
the metallurgical needs of India’s steel giants. To orchestrate this international synergy, 
we have established a new strategic hub in Dubai (United Arab Emirates), which serves 
as our tracking centre for mineral developments across the Middle East, North Africa, and 
Australia.

VALUE CHAIN  |  From exploration to 
customer industriesA CONNECTED CHAIN OF 
VALUE
NMDC’s value chain begins long before ore is mined 
and continues well beyond production. It starts with 
understanding the orebody, progresses through mine 
planning, extraction, processing and evacuation, and 
reaches its economic purpose when iron ore supports 
steelmakers and customer industries. This connected 
chain defines the Company’s role in India’s industrial 
economy: converting mineral potential into reliable 
raw-material supply.
ORE BODY KNOWLEDGE 
SHAPES EVERY DECISION
Exploration and resource assessment provide the 
foundation. Orebody knowledge shapes mine design, 
production sequencing, quality planning, equipment 
deployment and long-term capacity decisions. For a 
mining company of NMDC’s scale, stronger geological 
understanding is not only a technical capability; it is 
a strategic control. It enables the Company to plan 
extraction responsibly, maintain product consistency 
and protect the long-term value of its mineral assets.
OPERATING DISCIPLINE 
CONVERTS PLANS INTO 
OUTPUT
The next stage is disciplined mine development and 
production. In FY 2025-26, NMDC produced 53.16 MT 
of iron ore and recorded sales of 50.24 MT, reinforcing 
the strength of its operating base. This performance 
reflects the coordinated functioning of mine planning, 
drilling and blasting, excavation, haulage, crushing, 
screening, stockpile management, loading and 
dispatch. Each stage affects the next. Higher output 
creates value only when ore quality, equipment 
availability, processing capacity and evacuation 
readiness move in alignment.

PROCESSING FOR QUALITY 
AND CONSISTENCY
Processing and beneficiation strengthen the link 
between mining output and customer requirements. 
Screening, crushing and material-handling systems 
help convert mined ore into dispatchable product 
with the quality and consistency required by steel 
producers. NMDC’s ongoing investments in screening 
plants, crushing systems, conveyors, slurry pipeline 
infrastructure and rail connectivity are designed to 
reduce bottlenecks and improve the reliability of this 
flow from pit to plant to customer.
EVACUATION CONNECTS 
MINES TO MARKETS
Evacuation is a critical value-creation link. A tonne of 
ore becomes economic value only when it reaches 
the customer on time and in the required grade. 
Rail-line doubling, loading systems, stockpile visibility 
and logistics monitoring strengthen NMDC’s ability 
to move material reliably from mining complexes to 
consuming industries. This is especially important as 
India’s steel sector expands and customers require 
dependable supply from domestic sources.
DIGITAL CONTROL ACROSS 
THE CHAIN
Digitalisation is adding a new layer of control 
across the value chain. Digitally enabled drilling 
and blasting, real-time stockpile management, 
Unified mine logistic management and surveillance 
system, digital twins and enterprise sustainability 
management platforms to improve visibility across 
operations. These systems help management connect 
production conditions, inventory, logistics, safety 
and environmental parameters into a more informed 
operating view.MANAGING 
INTERDEPENDENCIES
The value chain also carries important 
interdependencies. Capital investment in processing 
or logistics may reduce near-term financial flexibility, 
but it strengthens manufactured and intellectual 
capital over time. Higher production supports 
customers and national development, but it also 
requires stronger safety systems, environmental 
management, community engagement and statutory 
compliance. NMDC’s operating model recognises 
these linkages and treats value creation as an 
integrated flow rather than a sequence of isolated 
activities.
BUILDING READINESS FOR 
GROWTH
As NMDC advances towards its long-term capacity 
ambition, the strength of this value chain will 
determine the quality of growth. The Company’s focus 
is to deepen ore body knowledge, expand production 
capability, improve processing and evacuation 
readiness, and serve customer industries with reliable 
supply. In doing so, NMDC continues to connect 
India’s mineral resources with the infrastructure, 
manufacturing and industrial capacity that power 
national progress.

The financial year concluding 31st March 2026 represents 
a shift in the chronology of NMDC Limited. Our successful 
breaching of the 50 million tonne annual production 
threshold and finishing with 53+ million tonne, is not a 
solitary operational achievement but the logical outcome 
of an organisational architecture designed for high-velocity 
scaling and a market strategy precisely aligned with India’s 
industrial resurgence. As we transition into the era of NMDC 
2.0, we recognize that physical scale alone is insufficient; 
it must be synchronised with digital “Decision Intelligence” 
and a collaborative stakeholder ecosystem that grants 
us the social licence to grow. This chapter delineates the 
internal and external forces that constitute our momentum, 
ensuring that NMDC remains the primary resource 
guarantor for a self-reliant Viksit Bharat.Every element of this architecture is 
designed to convert India’s mineral wealth 
into “Inclusive Prosperity,” ensuring that 
as NMDC scales, the nation’s economic 
pulse strengthens.
Our legacy of mining in harmony with nature has laid a 
foundation, but the momentum required for 100 million 
tonnes demands that we move beyond legacy practices 
and adopt a new mindset. I. MARKET CONTEXT: ANCHORING INDIA’S INDUSTRIAL 
RESURGENCE
NMDC operates at the fundamental 
core of India’s economic machinery. The 
external landscape is currently defined 
by the ambitious National Steel Policy 
2017, which targets a 300 MT crude 
steel capacity by the end of the decade. 
This sovereign goal necessitates an 
iron ore requirement of approximately 
435–445 MTPA, positioning NMDC 
as the critical catalyst for the nation’s 
manufacturing mission. We are navigating 
a market context characterised by rapid 
urbanisation, massive infrastructure 
development, and a significant shift 
toward “Green Steel” production.
The demand for high-grade iron ore, 
a segment where NMDC maintains 
a definitive competitive advantage 
with Fe content exceeding 64%, is 
projected to reach unprecedented levels. 
Simultaneously, the 2025-26 fiscal year 
has witnessed an intensified global 
focus on critical mineral security. By 
operationalising our Coal Division in India 
and exploring lithium and gold interests in 
Australia, we have strategically insulated 
our enterprise from the cyclical volatilities 
of the global iron ore market, ensuring 
long-term financial fortitude for our 
shareholders.

At NMDC, we adopt a “Synergistic

STRATEGIC CONTEXT
STRATEGIC PILLARS CONTINUED
SCALE EXPANSION – POWERING THE NATIONAL 
STEEL ASPIRATION
Our primary strategic pillar is the calculated scaling of India’s resource capacity to ensure 
the nation’s 300 MT crude steel aspiration is anchored by a resilient supply chain. Having 
crossed the 50 MT milestone in FY2026, NMDC is now aggressively executing a production 
ramp-up plan to reach 72 MTPA from existing iron ore mines, complemented by 28 MTPA 
from the NMDC-CMDC Limited (NCL) Joint Venture assets. This scale-up is underpinned 
by a Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) roadmap designed to eliminate logistics bottlenecks 
through the commissioning of the Slurry Pipeline Project and the doubling of the Kirandul-
Kothavalasa (KK) railway line. By transitioning from 34 MT in FY 2020-21 to 50+ MT, we have 
demonstrated that NMDC is not merely a participant in the market but the primary guarantor 
of India’s industrial resurgence.PILLAR I

PILLAR IIIOPERATIONAL MODERNISATION – DIGITISING THE 
CORE OF MINING
The transformation into NMDC 2.0 is driven by the strategic elevation of digital technology 
from a support function to a core pillar of “Decision Intelligence”. Central to this pillar is Project 
Kalpataru, our enterprise-wide implementation of SAP S/4 HANA, which enables real-time 
oversight of every facet of our operations. We are engineering “Smart Mines” equipped with 
Fleet Management Systems (FMS), 3D volumetric laser scanners, and autonomous sampling 
and analysis tools to enhance productivity and safety. This digital architecture, nurtured by our 
UNIDO-recognised R&D Centre, ensures that NMDC remains at the global forefront of technical 
mining excellence, utilizing data to optimize resource eco-efficiency and minimize mineral waste.
PILLAR IVVALUE-CHAIN BROADENING – DIVERSIFYING FOR 
MINERAL SECURITY
Recognising the strategic imperative of resource diversification, our fourth pillar focuses 
on NMDC’s evolution into a multi-mineral powerhouse. In FY2026, we achieved the historic 
operationalisation of our Coal Division with the commencement of commercial production at 
the Tokisud North coal block in Jharkhand, providing a vital counter-cyclical revenue stream 
and energy security for the nation. Furthermore, our diversification roadmap extends beyond the 
Indian subcontinent to include gold mining in Australia and the exploration of critical minerals 
like lithium and cobalt. This strategic broadening of our portfolio ensures that NMDC’s financial 
fortitude remains resilient against the cyclical volatilities of the global iron ore market while 
supporting the National Critical Mineral Mission.PILLAR IIDISCIPLINED DECARBONISATION – THE NET ZERO 
TRANSITION
As we expand our physical footprint, we are simultaneously decoupling our industrial growth 
from its environmental impact. Our strategy integrates the “Natural Capital trade-off,” wherein 
we balance intensive mineral extraction with large-scale biodiversity restoration - exemplified by 
the planting of over 3.0 million trees and the implementation of site-specific conservation plans 
near sensitive ecological zones like the Panna Tiger Reserve. By investing in renewable energy 
projects, such as wind power and grid-connected solar plants, we are ensuring that the 100 
million tonne journey is synonymous with a “Green Growth” philosophy.

Brownfield Optimisation: We 
are enhancing the Environmental 
Clearance (EC) limits of our core 
complexes at Bailadila (Chhattisgarh) 
and Donimalai (Karnataka). We have 
submitted applications to increase 
EC limits by 50% for Deposits 5 and 11 
at Bacheli, aiming for a total complex 
capacity of 30–35 MTPA over the 
medium term.
Greenfield and JV Expansion: A 
significant portion of our 100 MTPA 
target will be delivered through 
the development of Deposit-13 and 
Deposit-4 via our Joint Venture

cumulative production profile.
Asset-wise Contribution Path: To

is transforming its approach to 
machinery, material, and manpower 
planning, ensuring that each mine 
complex has a dedicated asset-
level roadmap to scale output while 
maintaining world-class cost-
competitiveness.
The Evacuation Masterplan: 
Building India’s Green Corridor
Scaling production to 100 MTPA 
is physically impossible without a 
concomitant revolution in logistics 
evacuation. NMDC is executing a 
high-velocity infrastructure roadmap 
- funded by an ambitious CAPEX plan 
- to ensure that pit-to-port bottlenecks 
are permanently eliminated.Phase-1 Slurry Pipeline: At 31st March 2026, 135.3 km slurry pipeline from Bacheli to 
Nagarnar was 94% complete, with 134.28 km pipeline laid. On commissioning it will provide 
a low-carbon, 15 MTPA evacuation channel that recovers iron ore fines and reduces reliance 
on road transport.
KK-Line Doubling: We are supporting the doubling of the 150 km Kirandul-Kothavalasa (KK) 
railway line, which is designed to augment evacuation capacity from the Bailadila sector from 
the current 28 MTPA to over 60 MTPA.
Intermediate Stockyards: To ensure an uninterrupted supply to our customers, we have 
operationalised an intermediate iron ore stockyard at Kumarmaranga in Chhattisgarh, 
enhancing our supply chain resilience.
Sustainable Scale: Harmonising Production with Ecological Restoration
NMDC recognises that reaching 100 MTPA necessitates a sophisticated management of the 
“Natural Capital trade-off”. We do not view our growth in isolation from our environmental 
footprint. Our Vision 2030 is inherently linked to our internationally benchmarked Net 
Zero Strategy and Roadmap, ensuring that as we scale our manufactured capital, we 
simultaneously restore our natural capital through large-scale biodiversity projects and zero 
liquid discharge (ZLD) systems. This “Green Growth” philosophy is the defining standard for 
NMDC 2.0, where efficiency is not just a goal, but a moral and operational mandate.Our compass points north - toward 
innovation, sustainability, and a 100 million 
tonnes strong future for India.

NMDC enters the next stage of Vision 2030 from a stronger 
operating base. FY 2025-26 iron ore production reached 53.16 
MT, 20.6% above the previous year, and the Company became 
the first Indian iron ore producer to cross the 50 MT annual 
threshold. The immediate production target is 60 MT in FY 
2026-27; the longer-term ambition is to build 100 MTPA of iron 
ore production capacity by FY 2030. These measures should be 
read carefully. Current output, next-year production and future 
installed capacity describe different stages of the pathway.The strategic need is clear. India's steel-production capacity 
is envisaged to reach 300 MTPA by FY 2030-31, increasing 
the importance of dependable domestic ore supply. NMDC's 
response combines brownfield expansion of existing complexes 
with greenfield development through NMDC-CMDC Limited, its 
joint venture with Chhattisgarh Mineral Development Corporation. 
By the end of FY 2025-26, the Company had 64.8 MTPA of 
standalone environmental-clearance capacity, supplemented 
by 17 MTPA for the joint venture's Deposits 4 and 13. Clearance 
capacity is a necessary permission to operate; it becomes 
productive capacity only when mining, processing, people and 
evacuation are ready.

THE ROADMAP IS AN INTEGRATED RELEASE 
PLAN
A mine can hold ore and environmental clearance, yet remain constrained by crushing, screening, loading, rail, slurry movement, 
water, power, land or community interfaces. Vision 2030 therefore has to be governed as a release plan: each asset reaches its next 
capacity step only when the linked packages and operating controls reach readiness. This shifts attention from isolated project 
percentages to the critical path across the value chain.

We must view NMDC Limited not merely 
as a mining company, but as a complex 
ecosystem where relationships, actions, 
and resources are meticulously woven 
together to ensure the company remains 
strong even during global economic shifts. 
This resilience is built upon three specific 
cornerstones: who we work with, what we 
do every day, and the unique strengths we 
possess.
THE SYNERGY OF STRATEGIC PARTNERSHIPS
The first pillar consists of our Key 
Partners, which are essentially the deep-
rooted relationships that grant us the 
“social licence” to operate. Because we 
are owned by the government through 
the Ministry of Steel, we act as a national 
champion rather than just a private 
business. This partnership ensures that 
our goals are perfectly aligned with the 
long-term industrial needs of the country. 
Furthermore, our collaborations with state 
governments and our specialized joint 
ventures - specifically the partnership with 
the Chhattisgarh Mineral Development 
Corporation - are vital. They are the keys 
that unlock access to some of the most 
valuable mineral deposits in the world. 
By working together, we overcome the 
complex challenges of land use and 
regulatory approvals, ensuring that the 
nation’s hidden mineral wealth is brought 
to the surface for the benefit of all citizens.
THE EVOLUTION OF OPERATIONAL ACTIVITIES
The second pillar is our Key Activities, 
which represent the heart of our daily 
operations. Historically, our identity 
was defined solely by the extraction 
of high-quality iron ore. However, true 
resilience requires the ability to diversify, 
and we have now evolved into a multi-
mineral powerhouse. The most significant 
transformation in this regard is our expansion into the energy sector through 
our newly established Coal Division. By 
beginning to mine coal domestically, we 
are performing a dual service: we are 
providing the essential energy required to 
keep India’s industrial engines running, 
and we are creating a “counter-cyclical” 
income stream. In layman’s terms, this 
means that if the global price of iron ore 
fluctuates or drops, our coal business 
provides a steady financial cushion that 
keeps our overall company stable and 
profitable.
THE FUSION OF NATURAL AND INTELLECTUAL 
RESOURCES
The final pillar consists of our Key 
Resources, which are the essential 
“ingredients” that allow us to outperform 
our global competitors. This begins with 
our natural endowment - we possess 
vast quantities of iron ore that is globally 
recognized for its extreme purity and high 
quality. Because our ore is so rich in iron 
and contains very few impurities, it is 
highly sought after by steelmakers and is 
much more efficient to process than the 
lower-quality ore found elsewhere.
However, raw materials alone are not 
enough in the modern world. The 
“Resilience” of our model is increasingly 
driven by our “Human Capital” - our 
people. We are moving away from 
traditional, manual mining and toward 
a future defined by “Smart Mining”. This 
means our workers are no longer just 
operating heavy machinery, they are 
becoming digital experts trained to use 
advanced technology and real-time data 
systems to oversee every aspect of the 
mine. This fusion of the earth’s natural 
riches with the digital intelligence of our 
workforce ensures that we mine not just 
for volume, but for the highest levels of 
safety and environmental harmony.VALUE PROPOSITION AND STAKEHOLDER 
CENTRICITY
NMDC’s core Value Proposition lies in 
being the world’s lowest-cost producer of 
premium iron ore, providing the bedrock 
for India’s 300 MT crude steel aspiration. 
We maintain Customer Relationships 
through radical transparency, utilizing the 
DARPAN portal for real-time engagement 
and quality assurance. Our Channels 
are defined by high-velocity evacuation 
infrastructure, including the 135 km slurry 
pipeline and the doubling of the KK-
railway line, which permanently eliminate 
logistics bottlenecks. This architecture 
ensures that our Cost Structure remains 
globally competitive while our Revenue 
Streams diversify into coal, gold, and 
critical minerals.
VALUE CREATION PHILOSOPHY OVER TIME
NMDC Limited’s value creation philosophy 
is a multi-temporal architecture that 
synchronises immediate operational 
agility with deep-seated national 
aspirations, ensuring that every tonne of 
mineral extracted serves as a definitive 
catalyst for sovereign prosperity. THE PILLARS OF RESILIENCE

The Medium Term
Transitioning into the medium-term, our value drivers are concentrated 
on the aggressive execution of the asset-wise roadmap toward 100 
million tonnes per annum (MTPA), underpinned by the ramp-up of 
existing mechanized complexes and the successful operationalisation 
of our Coal Division in Jharkhand to provide vital energy security and 
counter-cyclical revenue resilience. Simultaneously, our medium-term 
strategy is defined by the “Net Zero. Net Growth.” mandate, where 
we are committed to meeting interim milestones, to ensure that our 
manufactured capital expansion is successfully decoupled from its 
environmental footprint.
The Long Term
In the long-term perspective, NMDC’s philosophy transcends 
simple quantitative growth to position the enterprise as the 
primary resource supplier for India’s 300 MT crude steel 
aspiration, effectively doubling the nation’s industrial strength 
and anchoring the economic resurgence of a self-reliant 
Viksit Bharat. We ensure the preservation of natural capital 
and the fulfilment of intergenerational equity, cementing 
a legacy where industrial scaling is performed in sacred 
harmony with the environment for the prosperity of future 
generations.

and respond to the issues that matter most to our

Annual Report continues to rely upon our robust, Board-approved

disclosures. We recognise that the path to doubling our capacity to 100 
million tonnes by 2030 requires more than physical expansion; it demands a 
sophisticated equilibrium between industrial scaling and the management of 
environmental and social imperatives. This chapter serves as the definitive 
audit of the material landscape that governs NMDC 2.0, translating complex 
stakeholder expectations into actionable value drivers.

OUR MATERIALITY PROCESS:  
THE SYNERGISTIC APPROACH
In accordance with the Global 
Reporting Initiative (GRI) 3-1 
standards, our process for 
determining material topics remains 
rooted in a five-stage architectural 
framework: Identification, Relevance, 
Consultation, Management 
Inputs, and Final Prioritisation. We 
engage with nine key stakeholder 
groups - including employees, 
customers, investors, suppliers, 
regulatory authorities, NGOs, local communities, industry associations, and the media - to ensure a 360-degree 
perspective on our enterprise impacts. These engagements are conducted 
through high-touch channels such as town halls, annual general meetings, 
and customised survey questionnaires designed to quantify the “Influence 
on Stakeholder Assessment” against the “Significance of Economic, 
Environmental, and Social Impacts”.
Audit Confirmation: 
The 21 topics surveyed in the 2025-26 cycle have been reviewed 
and validated by Bureau Veritas as part of our reasonable assurance 
engagement, providing investors with verified data for their own ESG 
evaluations.

Profitability widened the choices
NMDC entered FY 2025-26 with a demanding financial equation. It had to support a step-up in iron ore production, continue a large 
mine-and-logistics build-out, fund the working requirements of a broader operating mix and maintain shareholder returns—all while 
remaining exposed to commodity prices, statutory levies and project timing. The year’s outcome materially improved the Company’s 
room to manoeuvre. Revenue from operations rose by 33.3% to `31,553.70 crore, profit after tax increased by 10.9% to `7,421.24 crore 
and operating cash flow more than tripled to `4,926.12 crore.
The value of this performance lies not only 
in the higher absolute numbers. It lies in 
what they allow NMDC to do next. Higher 
earnings increase the pool of internally 
generated capital available for expansion; 
stronger cash flow reduces the extent to 
which project delivery must rely on external 
funding; and a larger net-worth base gives 
the balance sheet more capacity to absorb 
market or execution shocks. Financial 
capital therefore sits behind each of NMDC’s 
other capitals: it pays for processing and 
evacuation assets, digital systems, skills, 
safety controls, community programmes 
and environmental management before 
those investments begin to produce their 
intended return.Financial momentum broadened the funding base

Revenue quality: scale first, mix 
second
Iron ore remained the economic centre 
of the portfolio. Domestic iron ore sales 
contributed `24,723.45 crore, or 78.4% 
of revenue from operations. Hot rolled 
coil sales added `3,960.86 crore, while 
domestic and export pellet sales together 
contributed `2,860.29 crore. This mix 
broadened the sources of reported 
revenue during the year, but it should not 
be mistaken for equal earnings quality 
across activities: the Board’s Report 
discloses sales values, not comparable 
segment margins or cash conversion. The 
investor-relevant conclusion is therefore 
measured—NMDC’s top line became more 
diversified, while its financial strength 
continued to depend substantially on the 
scale, realisation and cost position of iron 
ore.
The relationship between revenue and 
profit also deserves interpretation. 
Revenue grew by 33.3%, but profit before 
tax rose by 9.2%. The difference indicates 
that volume and mix expansion did not 
Cash conversion created allocation 
headroom
Net cash generated from operating 
activities rose to `4,926.12 crore from 
`1,577.36 crore. That improvement 
mattered because the investment 
programme was already consuming flow through to pre-tax earnings at the same rate. The chapter does not attribute this 
gap to a single unverified cause; instead, it frames the management task correctly: 
convert higher operating scale into durable margin through cost control, price and sales 
discipline, logistics efficiency and careful management of the wider product mix. Growth 
is financially useful when it improves cash generation after absorbing the costs required 
to produce and deliver it.
FY 2025-26 revenue composition. Product mix is shown as reported sales value and does

Shareholders also participated in the year’s performance. NMDC paid dividends of `3,077.13 crore 
during FY 2025-26, compared with `2,901.30 crore in the previous year. The Company declared and 
paid an interim dividend of `2.50 per share and recommended a final dividend of `1.00 per share, 
subject to shareholder approval. It also transferred `1,000 crore from profit to the General Reserve. 
These decisions reveal the central allocation balance: distribute a meaningful share of current value, 
retain sufficient strength for an asset-heavy growth programme and avoid allowing either objective to 
crowd out operating liquidity.
Capital allocation follows operating readiness
NMDC’s Vision 2030 envisages iron ore production capacity of 100 MTPA. As at 31st March 2026, the 
Company had secured environmental-clearance capacity of 64.8 MTPA, supplemented by 17 MTPA 
through the NMDC-CMDC joint venture across Deposit-13 and Deposit-4. Closing the remaining 
capacity gap requires coordinated investment across mine augmentation, processing, evacuation, 
housing and digital capability. During the year, execution advanced on Screening Plant III at Kirandul, 
Screening Plant II at Donimalai, the slurry pipeline project, crushing and conveying facilities and 
railway infrastructure. Each project draws cash before it generates throughput, making sequencing 
as important as sanction.
The appropriate discipline is stage-gated rather than purely budget-led. A processing plant cannot 
create value if mine readiness, utilities or evacuation lag; a rail or slurry system cannot release its full 
benefit unless upstream ore and downstream handling are available; and a digital platform cannot 
improve decisions if data ownership and user adoption remain weak. Financial capital is protected 
when projects are tested against permissions, engineering maturity, contracting, interdependent 
packages, commissioning readiness and expected cash generation. This is why NMDC’s Digital 
Project Management Unit, which monitors projects and packages above `30 crore, is also a financial-
control mechanism: earlier visibility over slippage can protect capital productivity.
Liquidity is a strategic reserve
Rapid expansion can make a profitable Company cash-constrained if working capital and 
construction outflows move ahead of collections and commissioning. NMDC’s financial-risk 
framework therefore matters alongside headline profitability. The audited statements describe credit 
assessment, ageing and expected-credit-loss review, rolling cash-flow forecasts, treasury limits and 
the management of surplus funds under applicable guidelines and Company policy. These controls 
are designed to preserve the ability to meet operating obligations, withstand volatility and continue 
priority projects without being forced into value-destructive financing or delayed maintenance.RAPID EXPANSION can make a

The stronger FY 2025-26 net-worth position—`33,835.62 crore, up 14.4%—provides a larger 
cushion, but it does not remove commodity, execution or transition risk. Iron ore realisations and 
demand can change faster than a multi-year project can be rescheduled. Statutory costs can alter 
mine economics. Receivables can absorb cash even while revenue grows. Energy transition and 
environmental compliance can add near-term expenditure while protecting longer-term continuity. 
The financial-capital story is therefore not one of surplus cash waiting to be spent; it is one of 
competing claims that must be prioritised against risk-adjusted value.
Road ahead: convert strength into returns
The next test is the quality of deployment. NMDC must keep funding the assets that remove real 
operating constraints, complete high-progress projects before fragmenting capital across too many 
new starts and protect maintenance and safety expenditure during the build-out. The Company 
must also continue to distinguish capacity, commissioned capacity, operating throughput and sales 
evacuation in its investment decisions. These are different stages of value creation, and financial 
returns emerge only when they align.
For investors, the most useful evidence will be a clearer bridge from annual capex to project 
milestones, commissioning, incremental throughput, cash conversion and return on capital 
employed. FY 2025-26 strengthened the financial platform: revenue, earnings, cash flow and net 
worth all increased. The enduring outcome will depend on whether that platform is converted into 
assets that start on time, operate reliably and generate sufficient cash to fund the next phase while 
continuing to reward shareholders.

The asset system moved more ore
FY 2025-26 demonstrated what 
manufactured capital is meant to do: 
convert geological resources and installed 
capability into a larger, deliverable volume 
of product. Iron ore production reached 
53.16 MT, up 20.6%, while sales increased 
by 13.2% to 50.24 MT. The difference 
between the two growth rates is a 
reminder that production alone does not 
define the strength of a mining system. Ore must pass through drilling, blasting, loading, crushing, screening, quality control, 
stockpiling and dispatch; the weakest stage can limit the value created by all the others.
This operating reality shapes NMDC’s Vision 2030 build-out. The ambition is not a 
single mine-capacity number but a coordinated network of brownfield augmentation, 
new deposits, processing facilities and evacuation infrastructure. By 31st March 2026, 
NMDC had environmental-clearance capacity of 64.8 MTPA, with a further 17 MTPA at 
the NMDC-CMDC joint venture’s Deposit-13 and Deposit-4. Turning that permissioned 
capacity into reliable production requires plants, conveyors, railway lines, slurry 
systems, utilities and people to be ready together. Manufactured capital is therefore 
managed as a chain, not as an inventory of projects.
Kirandul: adding capacity and flow
At the Kirandul Complex, Screening Plant III reached 82% overall progress by year-end. The Rapid 
Wagon Loading System package had been completed and was operating, while work continued 
on the main receiving substation, dry circuit, wet circuit and miscellaneous buildings. The loading 
system begins to strengthen dispatch capability, but the project’s full value depends on the 
remaining technological and supporting packages being completed, integrated and commissioned. 
Reporting a single progress percentage is useful; understanding which packages are already 
productive and which still govern the critical path is more useful.
The new crushing plant and downhill conveyor system for Deposits 14 and 11C was at an earlier 
stage, with 16% progress at 31st March 2026. These assets are intended to move ore from 
the deposit through crushing and controlled downhill conveying rather than relying only on 
conventional haulage. The near-term manufactured-capital effect is construction and work-in-
progress; the expected operating effect is a more continuous material flow, with potential benefits 
for haulage efficiency, equipment deployment and safety. Those benefits should be evidenced after 
commissioning rather than assumed from the technology choice.CAPITALS

by dumpers, and automatic sampling that

manufactured and intellectual capital converging: physical equipment is being designed 
to move material more efficiently, while automation improves the information used to 
control product quality.
The Company also awarded the operation, maintenance and development of the 1.2 MTPA 
Donimalai pellet plant under a 15-year revenue-sharing model. This expands the way an 
existing asset can be used without treating ownership alone as the source of value. The 
commercial outcome will depend on plant reliability, input availability, product quality, 
market conditions and the effectiveness of the operating arrangement. The asset becomes 
productive capital only when those operating conditions are met consistently.
Evacuation is the release mechanism
Of the 150.462 km route of doubling of the Kirandul–Jagdalpur railway line, 128 km had been 
completed and opened for traffic, with the remaining stretches expected to be completed in the 
current financial year. Once complete, the Board’s Report states that the project will increase the 
Bailadila sector’s rail evacuation capacity from 28 MTPA to 60 MTPA. The scale of that change 
illustrates why logistics is not a downstream support function; it determines how much mine and 
processing capacity can become saleable product.
The slurry pipeline project provides a second evacuation pathway. The 15 MTPA line from Bacheli 
to Nagarnar is being developed with a 2 MTPA ore-processing plant at Bacheli and a 2 MTPA 
pellet plant at Nagarnar. At 31st March 2026, 134.28 km of the 135.3 km pipeline had been laid. Site 
development and enabling works had been completed, and packages covering pipeline laying, 
pumping, pellet technology, ore processing and power were under execution. The remaining 
work is less visible than the completed kilometres but decisive: integration, utilities, testing and 
commissioning determine when infrastructure begins carrying commercial value.Selected project progress at 31st March 2026. Percentages reflect different project and package

Road ahead: commission the system
The manufactured-capital priority is to convert high project progress into commissioned, integrated 
and stable operation. That means closing remaining packages at the slurry pipeline and railway 
doubling, advancing the screening plants and crushing-conveying systems, and aligning mine 
readiness with processing and evacuation. It also means resisting a common reporting shortcut: 
equating physical completion with value creation. The decisive evidence arrives after commissioning—
throughput, availability, quality consistency, operating cost, safety performance and cash contribution.
As NMDC moves towards 100 MTPA, the central management question is not simply how much 
capacity can be sanctioned. It is how much dependable throughput can be created across the entire 
chain without allowing maintenance, people, permissions, community confidence or natural-resource 
controls to become the next bottleneck. FY 2025-26 showed both operating momentum and tangible 
project progress. The next phase must turn those advances into a balanced system that can produce 
and dispatch at a higher rhythm, repeatedly and safely.

A distributed geological capability
NMDC’s exploration wing at Raipur is 
supported by a Centre for Geostatistics 
and a remote-sensing laboratory at 
the Corporate Office in Hyderabad. 
Mine-planning wings operate at both 
corporate and project levels, using

Minesched for orebody modelling, reserve

This distribution is important: central

compare the model with daily operating 
evidence. The quality of the resource

field reconciliation remain connected.
Remote sensing broadens the field of 
view. It can help interpret terrain, landform 
and change across areas that are difficult 
to observe continuously from the ground. 
Drone surveys add higher-resolution 
operational data, while geostatistics helps 
convert sampled information into spatial 
estimates. The tools do not eliminate

explicit and manageable. Their value 
should be judged through decisions such

environmental attention is required.The knowledge-base indicators retain their distinct dates and scopes and are not

Process knowledge extends the resource
The R&D Centre at Hyderabad carries geological understanding into mineral processing 
and product development. The current-year MDA confirms its status as a Centre of 
Excellence recognised by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization and 
the Board’s Report confirms recognition by the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research. Its work spans mineral processing, beneficiation, pelletisation, process 
flowsheets, mineralogy, material handling, metallurgical studies of iron ore and coal, 
chemical analysis and process improvement. Laboratory and pilot-scale facilities allow 
an operating problem to be studied before a full-scale intervention is made.
This capability becomes more important as ore characteristics vary and lower-grade 
material must be considered. NMDC is developing facilities for dry beneficiation, which 
the MDA links to water-efficient processing of low-grade ores, and it is expanding 
capability to characterise and test critical minerals. The intellectual-capital effect is 
optionality: better characterisation and process routes may enable material that is 
currently difficult or uneconomic to be reassessed under different technical and market 
conditions. Realised value, however, depends on recovery, quality, energy, water, capital 
cost and scale—not on research activity alone.

Enterprise data becomes a shared 
asset
SAP S/4 HANA provides a common 
enterprise record across production,

human resources, safety and projects. 
Operational platforms add higher-
frequency information from the field:

and project progress. The emerging 
Digital Twin and Integrated Control and 
Command Centre are intended to connect

can make decisions more consistent 
across functions—but only if definitions, 
ownership, timestamps and interfaces are 
governed.Data quality is therefore a management responsibility, not an information-technology 
clean-up. A stockpile volume affects inventory and dispatch planning; a project 
milestone affects cash forecasts; a quality result affects blending and customer 
commitments; and an environmental reading can trigger compliance action. When 
the same concept is defined differently across systems, apparent visibility can hide 
real disagreement. Intellectual capital strengthens when the organisation knows 
which source is authoritative, how a metric is calculated, who can change it and how 
exceptions are resolved.
Governance protects the learning system
NMDC has established corporate and unit-level digitalisation teams to identify 
operational challenges and overcome them with digital interventions. This is a 
useful governance choice because it begins with a problem statement rather than 
a technology catalogue. The same logic should govern research and geological 
programmes: define the uncertainty or constraint, choose the appropriate method, 
establish the evidence required for a decision and record what changed. A portfolio view 
can then distinguish solutions that should be scaled, refined, held or stopped.

Intellectual assets also introduce risk. Connected systems expand cyber exposure; 
models can be used beyond the conditions in which they were validated; experienced 
people can leave before knowledge is transferred; and patents or reports can remain 
detached from operating priorities. Controls should therefore cover access, model 
validation, documentation, retention, succession and benefits realisation. The aim is not 
to freeze knowledge, but to make it reusable and challengeable.
Road ahead: compound the evidence
The next phase for NMDC is to connect geological, process and operating learning 
more deliberately. Exploration outcomes should update the resource model and mine 
plan; operating reconciliation should challenge the model; R&D should focus on the 
constraints that limit recovery, water or energy performance; and digital platforms 
should make the resulting decisions visible. This creates a compounding loop in which 
every campaign, blast, sample and pilot contributes to the next decision rather than 
remaining in a separate file or system.
FY 2025-26 strengthened the disclosed knowledge base through additional drilling, 
a current resource estimate, expanded digital deployment and confirmed R&D 
capabilities. The enduring advantage will not be measured by the volume of data 
or the number of tools. It will be measured by lower uncertainty, faster learning and 
better decisions—particularly as NMDC develops new deposits, brings coal assets into 
operation, handles more varied material and scales towards 100 MTPA.

At 31st March 2026, NMDC had 5,730 
permanent people: 1,546 executives and 
4,184 workers under the BRSR categories. 
This was a modest increase from 5,677 
in the previous year, with the mix shifting 
towards workers as permanent executives 
declined and permanent workers 
increased. The Board’s Report records HR 
productivity of 5,957 tonnes per employee, 
based on the 12-month average of regular 
and contractual personnel. The measure 
reflects the year’s higher production, but 
it should be read alongside safety, skills 
and operating context; productivity is 
not durable if it is achieved by increasing 
exposure or deferring capability.Reskilling follows the operating architecture
The learning agenda is beginning to reflect NMDC’s changing operating environment. 
Corporate HRD included practical data-analytics training in Excel and Power BI, 
programmes on contracts, vigilance, labour codes and Vision 2030, and leadership 
development covering strategic thinking, innovation, digital transformation, change 
management, sustainability, ESG and AI-enabled business transformation. At project 
level, training centres support statutory basic, refresher and skilled-worker programmes. 
The value of this portfolio lies in connecting enterprise knowledge with the specific 
tasks people perform at mines, plants and projects.
At NMDC, skill-upgradation training during FY2026 reached 59.96% of permanent 
executives, up from 33.75%, while coverage among permanent workers was 27.25%, 
slightly below 28.68%. Safety-training coverage reached 34.09% of permanent 
executives and 30.64% of permanent workers, compared with 23.51% and 28.32% 
respectively. Among other-than-permanent workers, 47.31% received safety training. 
Training coverage measures participation by category; it does not show proficiency or behaviour change.

Digital learning must be role-
specific
Smart mining changes roles differently. 
A drill-and-blast engineer must interpret 
terrain and model outputs; a surveyor 
must validate a stockpile model; a 
maintenance team must understand 
connected equipment and data quality; 
a supervisor must respond to alerts 
without surrendering judgement; and a 
finance or project manager must see how 
an operating exception affects cost and 
schedule. Training should therefore move 
beyond software navigation. It should 
use operating scenarios, define the limits 
of the model, rehearse overrides and 
connect the digital signal to the person 
accountable for action.
Formal performance and career-
development reviews covered 100% of 
permanent executives and workers in both 
years. This gives NMDC a mechanism 
to connect role expectations, skill gaps and development. The next quality test is whether the review translates into an 
individual learning pathway and deployment opportunity. Completion is an important 
control indicator; the outcome lies in improved readiness, succession depth and on-
job application. As new systems scale, those links should become more visible in the 
people scorecard.
The control framework is established
NMDC’s Corporate Occupational Health and Safety Policy applies across operations, and 
all mines are certified to ISO 45001:2018 as part of an Integrated Management System. 
Routine hazards are addressed through Safety Management Plans, standard operating 
procedures, Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment and Job Safety Analysis. Non-
routine work uses permits, task-specific assessments and supervisory approval. Internal 
safety audits occur twice a year, while equipment inspections are conducted quarterly.
Workers can report hazards through supervisory and site mechanisms and are 
empowered to stop work and remove themselves from serious risk without retaliation. 
Permit-to-work, toolbox talks, inspections and lock-out/tag-out support the control 
system. These mechanisms are necessary, but the FY 2025-26 outcome demonstrates 
that effectiveness must be judged at the point of work. The management response tests 
whether critical controls were understood, present and verified; whether contractor and 
employee standards aligned; whether leading indicators identified deterioration; and 
whether lessons reached every site.CAPITALS

Leadership continuity is an 
operating risk control
NMDC continued to institutionalise 
succession planning through identification 
of critical roles, competency mapping, 
readiness assessment, talent pools, 
career planning and periodic review. 
This is strategically material because 
mine, project, mineral-processing and 
safety roles carry experience that cannot 
be replaced quickly. Expansion and 
retirement can create simultaneous gaps. 
Succession becomes effective when a 
named successor receives experience 
before the vacancy arises, not when a list 
is produced after it occurs.
Leadership-development programmes 
focused on strategic decision-making, 
innovation, digital transformation, 
change and sustainable growth. The 
required leadership style is practical: 
managers must integrate project, people, 
safety, community and environmental 
consequences, not optimise one target 
in isolation. Cross-functional exposure, 
mentoring and job rotation can build that 
perspective if they are directed towards 
critical future roles. The measure of a 
leadership pipeline is readiness at the 
moment of need.Inclusion and welfare support continuity
Women represented 5% of executives and 7% of permanent workers; the Board’s 
Report recorded 374 women within the permanent workforce. Representation at Board 
and key-management levels was Nil at 31st March 2026 under the BRSR disclosure. 
These figures show that gender inclusion remains a material area for sustained action, 
particularly as technical and digital roles evolve. Recruitment pipelines, site facilities, 
career development and succession should be reviewed together so that participation is 
not limited to entry but extends into operational and leadership progression.
Remote-site continuity also depends on the conditions around work. NMDC provides 
education, health, accommodation, crèche and recreation facilities and is expanding 
township infrastructure at Kirandul, Donimalai and Bacheli. These investments affect 
attraction, retention and family stability in locations where the labour market and 
urban infrastructure are limited. Welfare should be managed as part of the employee 
value proposition, while its outcomes are assessed through retention, engagement, 
absenteeism and access rather than through assets alone.
Road ahead: capability with zero compromise
The immediate priority is to respond to the safety outcome with depth and transparency. 
Critical-control verification, incident and near-miss learning, contractor governance, 
supervisory presence and the quality of field-level risk assessment should be reviewed. 
Training should be refreshed where the evidence requires it, but training alone 
should not become the default response to a system or design failure. Engineering, 
maintenance, work planning and accountability must be examined together.
Alongside this, NMDC must accelerate role-specific reskilling for automated sampling, 
digital twins, AI-enabled blast design, mine logistics, project controls and SAP-enabled 
processes. The success measure is an adaptable workforce that can take on new 
technology, challenge it intelligently and operate at higher scale without normalising 
risk. Human capital will power NMDC’s next phase when productivity, learning, 
inclusion, wellbeing and safety reinforce one another—and when every shift returns 
people home safely.

Trust is part of operating continuity
NMDC operates in regions where the 
mine is a large economic, environmental 
and institutional presence. Communities 
experience both the opportunities created 
by employment, infrastructure and 
services and the disruption associated 
with land, traffic, dust, water, blasting 
and landscape change. The Company 
identifies community relations as an 
opportunity because acceptance in 
remote and tribal regions is critical to 
continuity. This is a practical definition of 
social licence: the ability to operate and 
expand with relationships strong enough 
to surface concerns early and resolve 
them credibly.The relationship cannot be managed through expenditure alone. CSR may address 
education, healthcare, nutrition, skills, infrastructure and livelihoods, but consultation 
and grievance response are what connect the programme to lived priorities. NMDC 
engages through Gram Sabhas, public consultations, village meetings, needs 
assessments, Panchayati Raj institutions, community representatives and local 
administration. The management task is to carry what is heard into project, operating 
and CSR decisions and then return with evidence of closure.
CSR builds capability across life stages
NMDC’s CSR obligation for FY 2025-26 was `166.30 crore. The Board approved projects 
above that amount, with a substantial share classified as multi-year ongoing projects; 
associated spending will therefore occur over approved implementation periods. This 
timing is important. An unspent balance linked to an ongoing project is not the same 
as an abandoned commitment, but it still requires milestone discipline. Communities 
experience delivery, not approval value. The programme should be followed from 
sanction through physical progress, service quality and outcome.CAPITALS

rather than a single intervention. The

Several programmes are designed to leave capability within the region. ITIs and the 
Polytechnic build technical skills; the nursing and medical-technology initiatives create 
professional pathways for tribal youth; the mid-day meal programme supports nutrition 
and school participation; and Aastha Gurukul and Saksham provide residential support 
to vulnerable and differently abled children. The strongest shared-value logic is visible 
where a local need and NMDC’s long-term operating context meet—skills, health and 
infrastructure that improve lives while strengthening the regional ecosystem around 
remote projects.
Inclusive procurement spreads economic participation
Relationship capital also sits in the supplier base. NMDC conducted 15 vendor meets 
and programmes covering quality, timely payment, ethical governance and SA8000 
expectations. It also engaged prospective micro and small entrepreneurs at Kirandul, 
Bacheli, Donimalai and Panna to explain procurement opportunities. In FY 2025-26, 
procurement from micro and small enterprises reached 36.18% of value against a 25% 
norm; procurement from SC/ST MSEs reached 5.23% against 4%; and women MSE 
procurement reached 4.47% against 3%.
The achievement is both social and operational. A more inclusive supplier base can 
create local economic opportunity and broaden competition; capable suppliers can 
also improve responsiveness in remote locations. Inclusion must be accompanied by 
quality, safety, delivery and integrity. Awareness programmes and trial opportunities help 
suppliers enter the system, while clear specifications, timely settlement and transparent 
tendering help them remain viable. The objective is durable participation, not only a 
year-end percentage.

Customer relationships reveal operating quality
NMDC’s customers are largely steel manufacturers whose operations depend on reliable 
volume, grade and delivery. Customer complaints in the ‘Other’ category increased from 19 
to 40, with two pending at year-end compared with none in the previous year. 
A complaint system creates value when it improves the underlying process. A quality 
concern may lead to sampling, blending or laboratory action; a delivery concern may 
reveal loading or rail constraints; a commercial concern may indicate documentation 
or communication gaps. Closing the individual complaint is necessary, but preventing 
recurrence is the relationship-capital outcome. Customers should be able to see both 
responsiveness and reliability over time.

Road ahead: make responsiveness measurable
NMDC should keep flagship programmes stable where continuity matters, while 
strengthening outcome and milestone measurement. Multi-year projects need visible 
delivery schedules; education and health programmes need outcome measures 
proportionate to their design; community concerns need ageing and closure data; 
suppliers need capability and compliance pathways; and customers need root-cause 
prevention. This does not require reducing relationships to a single score. It requires 
showing that the Company listens, acts and learns.
FY 2025-26 provides strong evidence of reach: substantial education and health 
programmes, inclusive procurement above norms and structured stakeholder 
channels. It also provides signals that deserve management attention, including 
higher customer complaints and the absence of quantified community-grievance 
performance. Social and relationship capital will strengthen when the scale of 
NMDC’s presence is matched by the quality of its response - and when stakeholders 
can trace the line from a concern raised to a decision changed.

Scale tests the quality of stewardship
Iron ore production rose by 20.6% to 53.16 MT in FY 2025-26. That achievement increased the amount of material moved 
and the demand placed on equipment, energy, water, land and environmental controls. Natural capital therefore cannot be 
described only through conservation programmes. It must be read alongside operating scale: whether resource use and 
emissions grow faster or slower than output, whether local impacts remain within permission and control, and whether 
rehabilitation progresses while the mine is active rather than being deferred to closure.
The year’s evidence is mixed in a useful way. Total energy consumption increased by 9.2% and Scope 1 and Scope 
2 greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 5.7%, but both grew more slowly than production and their physical intensities 
improved. Water consumption fell by 7.4% on the restated comparative basis and physical intensity declined from 0.21 
to 0.16 KL per tonne, even as total water withdrawal increased. The story is therefore neither unqualified improvement 
nor deterioration: NMDC produced more with lower reported intensity, while its absolute energy and emissions footprint 
remained larger.

Reuse and discharge require 
transparent boundaries
Certain dry-screening operations at 
Kirandul, Donimalai and Deposit-10/11A at 
Bacheli do not generate process effluent. 
Panna’s wet processing recycles water 
through tailings storage and recirculation 
and is described as operating under a 
Zero Liquid Discharge framework. Other 
locations use recirculation, effluent 
treatment and sewage treatment 
according to operational and regulatory 
requirements. The Company also reports 
higher treated discharge in FY 2025-26. 
These site differences should be kept 
visible; a control at one facility should not 
be implied to cover the enterprise.
Energy intensity improved, absolute 
demand rose
Total reported energy consumption 
reached 1.86 million GJ, of which fuel and 
non-renewable electricity accounted for 
the overwhelming majority. Renewable-
source energy consumed was 4,773 GJ, 
down from 5,916 GJ. The physical energy 
intensity improved from 0.039 to 0.035 GJ 
per tonne. This suggests that operating scale increased faster than energy use, but it also shows the transition challenge: 
efficiency is improving from a base still dominated by non-renewable energy, while the 
disclosed renewable contribution decreased during the year.
NMDC operates 10.5 MW of wind capacity at Chitradurga and 1.5 MW of rooftop 
solar across production units. Energy audits and efficiency measures complement 
this installed base. Renewable capacity, renewable energy consumed and avoided 
emissions are different measures; they should not be used interchangeably. Future 
reporting should connect capacity to generation, consumption, site demand and the 
emissions factor so the transition effect can be evaluated.
Emissions performance follows the same tension
Scope 1 emissions increased to 112,805 tCO2e from 103,482 tCO2e, and Scope 2 
emissions rose to 85,567 tCO2e from 84,202 tCO2e. Combined emissions reached 
198,372 tCO2e. Physical intensity nevertheless declined from 0.0042 to 0.0037. The 
improvement indicates more output per unit of reported emissions, but absolute 
decarbonisation has not yet occurred. For a growth company, both measures are 
material: intensity shows operating efficiency, while absolute emissions determine the 
size of the climate footprint.
Land management extends through the mine life
Mining changes landform and drainage and creates long-duration obligations. NMDC 
submits Mining Plans and Progressive Mine Closure Plans for operating leases to the 
Indian Bureau of Mines and must prepare a Final Mine Closure Plan before closure. 
The disclosed control system includes buttress walls, garland drains, check dams, 
settling ponds, waste-dump stabilisation and ongoing reclamation and plantation. These 
structures are not peripheral civil works: they manage erosion, sediment and stability 
and protect surrounding water and land.CAPITALS

Biodiversity is both ecological and 
operational
The BRSR identifies biodiversity and 
land management as a risk because 
habitat disturbance, poor reclamation or 
non-compliance can create restoration 
cost, conflict and operating constraints. 
NMDC’s response includes a Biodiversity 
Policy, collaboration with State Forest 
Departments, in-situ conservation, 
ecological monitoring, wildlife programmes, Environmental Impact Assessments and Environmental Management 
Plans. The governance challenge is to translate enterprise policy into site-specific 
baselines, objectives, buffers, progressive rehabilitation and evidence of condition.
Biodiversity is connected to water and community relationships. Drainage or erosion 
can affect downstream users; habitat change can alter livelihoods or cultural value; and 
restoration choices can influence long-term land use. This means environmental teams 
must be involved in mine design, waste-dump planning, project packages and closure 
decisions—not asked to mitigate a finished engineering plan. Natural capital is protected 
most efficiently when impacts are avoided or reduced before they require restoration.
Road ahead: manage absolute impact and intensity
NMDC’s next natural-capital scorecard should retain the balanced view demonstrated 
by the year’s data. Lower energy, water and GHG intensity are positive; higher absolute 
energy and emissions remain material. Water withdrawal should be linked to site 
stress and source; rehabilitation should show area and ecological condition; renewable 
capacity should be connected to generation and consumption; and mine growth should 
include the environmental infrastructure required to support it.
FY 2025-26 showed that higher output can be accompanied by better resource intensity. 
The enduring test is whether that efficiency continues as new deposits, coal assets, 
processing plants and evacuation systems come online—and whether absolute impact 
begins to bend down where technically and economically feasible. NMDC’s licence to 
sustain long-life mining depends on that double discipline: use each unit of natural 
capital more carefully and restore the systems affected by its use.Absolute GHG emissions increased; physical intensity improved
