2.1. Economic Overview
 2.1.1. Global Economy
  Global economy has been facing major headwinds due 
to ongoing conflict in the Middle East and associated 
supply chain disruptions. The IMF in its World Economic 
Outlook update released in April 2026 has projected 
global GDP to grow at 3.1% in 2026 & 3.2% in 2027 
against a growth of 3.4% in 2025. It has also highlighted 
the fact that the slowdown in growth and increase 
in inflation are expected to be more pronounced in 
emerging and developing economies1.
  Meanwhile, headline inflation is expected to rise to 
about 4.4% in 2026 as compared to 4.1% in 2025. Under 
severe scenarios (assuming energy market dislocations 
extending to next year), IMF predicts that the headline 
inflation can go as high as 6% & global economy can 
come close to experiencing a recession with growth of 
around 2%.

 2.1.2. Indian Economy
  India continues to remain one of the fastest-growing 
major economies globally, supported by strong domestic 
demand, prudent macroeconomic management and 
sustained policy reforms. Despite a challenging global 
environment characterized by geopolitical uncertainties, 
trade disruptions and financial market volatility, the 
Indian economy has demonstrated remarkable resilience 
and is expected to maintain its growth momentum 
during FY 2026-27.
1  World Economic Outlook Report | April 2026
2  P- Proje cted  As India enters FY27, the economic environment faces 
headwinds from growing tensions in the Middle East and 
trade policy uncertainty. However, the broader trajectory 
is expected to remain resilient. According to estimates 
by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), India’s GDP growth is 
projected at 6.6% in FY 2026-273, reinforcing its position 
as a key driver of global economic growth.
  The Government’s continued emphasis on capital 
expenditure, logistics enhancement, digital infrastructure, 
renewable energy and industrial competitiveness is 
expected to strengthen the country’s long-term growth 
prospects. Initiatives such as the National Manufacturing 
Mission, Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, PM 
Gati Shakti and Make in India are fostering domestic 
manufacturing capabilities and improving India’s 
attractiveness as a global investment destination.
  Inflationary pressures have intensified amid rising global 
energy prices and supply-side disruptions. The Reserve 
Bank of India (RBI) has revised its FY27 Consumer 
Price Index (CPI) inflation forecast upward to 5.1% from 
4.6%4, reflecting the impact of elevated crude oil prices 
and global supply constraints. Higher energy costs are 
exerting adverse spillover effects on the economy by 
increasing transportation, logistics and production costs 
across sectors. The country’s external sector remains 
resilient, underpinned by healthy foreign exchange 
reserves - $ 682.3 billion as on 29.05.20265.
  India remains a leading destination for global 
investment, supported by a liberal and business-friendly 
FDI framework. The country permits 100% foreign 
ownership in most sectors through the automatic route, 
encouraging investor confidence. As a result, foreign 
direct investment (FDI) inflows reached USD 94.53 
billion in FY 2025–26 — exceeded the previous record of 
USD 84.84 billion in FY 2021-22. However, net FDI inflows 
stood at USD 7.7 billion, as a significant portion of inflows 
was offset by higher repatriation of investments by 
foreign companies and increased overseas investments 
by Indian corporates6. Nevertheless, the strong growth in 
gross FDI underscores India’s continued attractiveness 
as a lucrative investment destination.
  India’s export sector continued to demonstrate resilience 
in FY 2025–26 despite ongoing geopolitical tensions and 
subdued global demand. Total merchandise and services 
exports reached USD 860.09 billion in FY 2025-26, up

2.2. Industry Overview
 2.2.1 Global Steel Industry
  Global crude steel production softened in 2025 at 1,849 
million tonnes8, ~ 5.8% below the peak global output of 
1,963 million tonnes in 20219. Key producers – including 
China, Japan, Russia and South Korea- recorded declines 
while India and the US recorded increase in crude steel 
production by 10.4% & 3% respectively.
  In 2025, China’s steel exports increased by 14.1%, 
reaching 133.6 million tonnes from 117.1 million tonnes in 
2024. Global apparent steel use has declined from 1,751

 2.2.2 Indian Steel Industry
  India’s steel industry continued its strong growth 
trajectory in FY26, supported by robust domestic demand 
from infrastructure, construction, manufacturing, 
automotive and capital goods sectors. Crude steel 
production increased to ~168 million tonnes during 
FY2614, registering a growth of around 10.7% over the 
previous year, while finished steel consumption rose by 
7-8% to about 164 million tonnes15. The sustained growth 
in steel consumption reflects the continued momentum 
in economic activity and the Government’s focus on 
infrastructure development.
  Driven by robust domestic demand, Indian steelmakers 
continued to expand their capacities during FY26, 
increasing the country’s total installed steelmaking 
capacity to ~220 MTPA. These investments, coupled with 
the ramp-up of existing facilities, further strengthened 
India’s position as the world’s second-largest crude 
steel producer. Despite this progress, per capita steel 
consumption in India reached 109 kg in 202516, well below 
the global average of 209 kg in 202517, underscoring 
considerable headroom for long-term demand growth. 
To unlock this potential, the country has set an ambitious 
target of raising per capita steel consumption to 160 kg 
by FY3118.

producer, NMDC continued to play a pivotal role in 
supporting the country’s growing steel industry’s iron ore 
demand. The Company achieved a historic milestone by 
becoming the first mining company in India to surpass 
the 50 million tonne annual production mark, recording 
its highest-ever iron ore production of 53.15 million 
tonnes, a growth of 21% over the previous year.
  On the trade front, FY26 marked a significant turnaround 
as India regained its status as a net exporter of finished 
steel. Finished steel exports increased to around 6.6 
million tonnes with a surge of 35.9%, while imports 
declined sharply by 31.7%19. The improvement was 
supported by stronger export demand from key markets 
in West Asia, Europe and Southeast Asia, coupled 
with policy measures aimed at safeguarding domestic 
industry interests. During the year, the Government 
imposed a 12% safeguard duty on select steel products 
to address the surge in low-priced imports and support 
domestic producers20.
  However, iron ore exports declined by ~13% to 26 million 
tonnes, while imports surged by more than 70% to 12 
- 12.5 million tonnes21 as iron ore production growth 
lagged the steel output growth.
  Looking ahead, the outlook for the Indian steel sector 
remains positive, driven by sustained investments in 
infrastructure, urbanisation, housing, transportation and 
renewable energy projects. Government initiatives such 
as PM Gati Shakti, National Infrastructure Pipeline, PM 
Awas Yojana and continued investments in railways, 
roads and logistics are expected to support long-term 
steel demand growth.
3. NMDC – Opportunities & Threats
a) Opportunities
 i) Envisaged growth in domestic steel production on 
account of the factors mentioned below would lead to 
higher demand for Iron Ore in the country:
 • Infrastructure and capital expenditure spending by the 
Government of India remains at a record high, with the 
Union Budget FY27 proposing capital outlay above `12.2 
lakh crore. Construction, infrastructure and real estate 
continue to account for over 60% of domestic steel 
consumption and are expected to boost the iron and 
steel sector demand in India.
19  PIB
20  PIB
21  BigMint • India’s per capita steel consumption at approximately 109 
kg remains well below the world average of ~209 kg22, 
providing substantial headroom for growth. Increasing 
urbanization, expanding rural infrastructure, multiple 
key initiatives by the government along with a host of 
consumption enablers are expected to drive up the steel 
demand in key end-use sectors. Government initiatives 
for Self-Reliant India creating new avenues to set-up new 
industries is leading to demand in iron and steel.
 • The Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for 
Specialty Steel in India expands on the original 2021 
framework (PLI 1.0) through subsequent phases like PLI 
1.1 and PLI 1.2. It aims to boost domestic value-added 
steel manufacturing, reduce import dependence and 
offer financial incentives ranging from 4% to 15%. PLI 
1.2 was launched on 04.11.2025, covering 22 product 
sub-categories under four product categories, namely: 
(i) Steel Grades for Strategic Sector, (ii) Commercial 
Grades – Category 1, (iii) Commercial Grades – Category 
2 and (iv) Coated & Wire Products. The scheme offers 
incentive rates ranging from 4% to 15% for a period of 
five years, commencing from FY 2025–26, with incentive 
disbursement starting from FY 2026–27. The Production 
Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for specialty steel 
continues to attract investment, with committed capex 
from major steel producers, directly expanding the iron 
ore demand base.
 • Government initiatives including Make in India 2.0, the 
semiconductor and electronics manufacturing push and 
the defence indigenization programme are attracting 
new industrial capacities that create downstream 
demand for steel and by extension, iron ore.
 • Rising vehicle production, including electric vehicles 
(EVs), is expected to increase demand for high-strength 
and specialized steel grades. Expansion of solar, wind, 
transmission infrastructure and energy storage projects 
requires significant quantities of steel. Dedicated 
freight corridors, multimodal logistics parks and port 
modernization can reduce transportation costs and 
improve competitiveness.
 • India’s target of 300 MTPA domestic steel capacity 
by 2030-31, as envisaged in the National Steel Policy, 
provides a long-term structural demand anchor for 
NMDC’s high-grade ore. NMDC’s ore is among the 
highest-grade lump ore available globally, positioning 
the company favourably as steelmakers optimise blast 
furnace burdens.

 ii) Favourable macroeconomic and policy environment 
supports medium-term growth:
 • IMF projects India’s GDP growth at 6.5% in FY2623,

economy and driving steel-intensive investment in

b) Threats
 i) Geopolitical instability, including the ongoing tensions in 
the Middle east & Russia-Ukraine conflict has created 
uncertainty in global commodity markets, supply chains 
and shipping costs, all of which can influence iron ore 
price benchmarks and trade flows.
 ii) Rising fuel cost due to supply shocks can impact margins 
as a significant proportion of mining fleet is diesel 
operated. Apart from fuel, supply chain disruptions may 
also delay scheduled import of equipment & HEMMs for 
operations, leading to delay in expansion projects.
 iii) Rising inflation can impact consumption and lead to 
23  IMF World Economic Outlook | Apr26fiscal tightening increasing the cost of borrowings 
affecting investments.
 iv) Allocation of iron ore blocks through Auction in Bailadila 
to players other than NMDC may exert pressure on 
already strained evacuation channels from the area.
 v) Uncertainty in export duties of iron ore, pellets can lead 
to volatility in the prices of iron ore, further leading to 
reduced iron ore demand.
 vi) Demand for Iron ore may fall in the international market 
in long term due to the decline in the Chinese steel 
production and shift towards EAF/IF route for recycling 
scrap steel.
 vii) New iron ore leases being auctioned and the amendments 
to MMDR Act allowing sale of all the iron ore production 
of captive mines in open market, after meeting their 
demand, is creating increased supply and competition in 
the market.
 viii) Indian iron ore industry will continue to be uncompetitive 
on a global level due to higher rates of royalty and other 
levies such as DMF, NMET, Export duty etc. as well as 
significantly higher logistics costs.
 ix) Potential adoption of state-level levies such Mineral 
Bearing Land and Mineral Rights Taxes could significantly 
increase statutory costs and adversely impact mining 
project economics.
 x) Increasing regulatory pressure on environment, health & 
safety and sustainability.
 NMDC’s business would continue to be affected by 
developments impacting the demand-supply scenario & 
price fluctuations of iron ore in both the global and domestic 
markets.

5. Outlook for NMDC
 NMDC proposes to augment its production capacity of iron 
ore to 100 MT by FY’30. It has also embarked on value addition 
projects by setting up a 1.2 MTPA pellet plant utilizing slimes 
in Karnataka NMDC-CMDC Limited (NCL), a JV company of 
NMDC Limited & CMDC Limited, has inaugurated & started 
operations at Deposit-4 in March 2026 and is expected 
to begin operations at Deposit-13 soon. NMDC has also 
developed an intermediate stockpile at Kumar Marenga 
near Jagdalpur to ensure an uninterrupted supply of ore to 
the customers. To augment evacuation capacity, NMDC is 
supporting the doubling of K-K line (Kirandul- Kotvatsala), 
constructing Slurry Pipeline, etc.
 NMDC has further diversified its business by beginning 
operations in one of its Coal Mine block, namely Tokisud 
North, Jharkhand in January 2026. Actions to operationalize 
the other allocated Coal Block, Rohne, are underway.
 NMDC has prepared its Diversification & International 
Expansion Strategy to venture into various identified minerals 
& geographies & will continue to look for opportunistic assets 
based on the recommendation & strategy in the formulated 
report. NMDC is reviewing various mineral asset projects in 
Africa, South America, MENA region etc as per the strategy. 
NMDC has opened its offices in Dubai, UAE and Sydney, 
Australia to give thrust on mineral scouting abroad.
 NMDC is committed to focusing on maintaining cost 
competitiveness in the global and domestic markets in a 
scenario where prices are expected to remain subdued. 
Further, NMDC is taking various initiatives towards automation & digitization of its operation to further improve its cost 
competitiveness.
 Along with robust strategic planning to support its growth 
agenda, NMDC continues to enhance organizational 
capabilities and other enablers to achieve its short-term and 
long-term objectives.
6. Risks and Concerns
 Geopolitical unrests like ongoing fights in the Middle East 
and the Russia-Ukraine war have created uncertainty in 
global commodity markets. It is pushing up shipping costs, 
raising fuel prices for mining fleets and causing supplychain 
delays that postpone equipment and HEMM imports. This is 
a matter of concern as it can affect input costs, ironore price 
benchmarks and trade flows. Any slowdown in domestic 
or global steel production due to economic downturns, 
trade restrictions, or reduced infrastructure spending may 
adversely affect iron ore demand.
 NMDC is exposed to sharp fluctuations in demand for its 
products and volatility in prices. Falling prices of iron ore, 
especially in international market will support the import 
by the steel players & exert pressure on domestic supply & 
prices. Fluctuations in international iron ore and steel prices 
can impact revenue realization and profitability.
 Timely enhancement of evacuation capacity in line with 
production plans also remains a potential concern. New 
players getting ore block allocation in the Bailadila region 
could impact production and inventory levels for NMDC.

 Introduction of Auction rule has increased risks for NMDC as 
its major customers have acquired captive mines in mineral-
rich states, mainly JSW & AM-NS. Both JSW & AM-NS are 
increasing production from newly acquired mines & planned 
to focus on other supply sources. This is likely to impact the 
market for NMDC over the medium to long term.
 In April 2026, the Government amended the Mineral Concession 
Rules to introduce a discounted pricing mechanism for sub-
threshold iron ore (below 45% Fe). By pegging the ASP of 
35-45% Fe ore at 75% of the standard benchmark, the rule 
reduces the royalty burden and incentivizes the utilization of 
low-grade resources. Operationally, this requires allocation of 
additional on-site storage space to separate sub-threshold 
ore from actual mine waste for future beneficiation.
 Increasing stakeholder focus on sustainability, carbon 
emissions, biodiversity conservation and responsible mining 
practices may necessitate additional investments and 
compliance measures.
 With NMDC commencing Coal Mining from allocated blocks, 
the opening of the Coal sector for Commercial mining will 
increase the competition for NMDC in the short to medium 
term.
 Increasing digitalization and interconnected operational 
systems expose the organization to cyber threats, data 
breaches and operational disruptions.
 Despite these challenges, NMDC continues to strengthen 
its operational resilience through resource expansion, 
digital transformation, sustainability initiatives, strategic 
diversification and prudent risk management practices, 
positioning the Company for sustainable long-term growth.

13. Environment:
 • Environmental monitoring studies are conducted through 
recognized laboratories of MoEFCC/ CPCB, covering 
all environmental parameters. Based on the results of 
environmental monitoring studies, it is concluded that 
all environmental parameters are well within the limits 
during FY 25-26. A total of 14 nos Continuous Ambient 
Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) have been 
installed at Bacheli complex (2 nos), Kirandul complex 
(9 nos) and Donimalai complex (3 nos) for recording of 
Ambient air quality parameters such as PM10, PM2.5, 
SO2, NOx and CO in real time.
 • Every year Carbon Footprint studies are being conducted 
for disclosure of Greenhouse Gas Emissions under 
Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). Water Audit is 
conducted at regular intervals at all projects of NMDC 
and recommendations of audit are being implemented to 
conserve water and to improve the efficiency of motors 
/ pumps, arrest leakages, etc.  Apart from this regular 
maintenance of water appurtenances is being done. • Sustainable Mining Initiative audit is being done at all 
Iron Ore Mining projects of NMDC and recommendations 
are being implemented.
 • The R&R works suggested by M/s Indian Council of 
Forest Research and Education (ICFRE, Dehradun) in 
the Environmental Management and Reclamation & 
Rehabilitation Plan for Kirandul Complex, Chhattisgarh 
and in Donimalai Complex, Karnataka are under 
implementation stage. 
 • R&D works in the field of air, water, solid waste etc. were 
undertaken by engaging institutes of repute such as ISM 
Dhanbad, NIT – Raipur and VNIT – Nagpur.
 • The environmental pollution control works are 
undertaken such as de-silting of check dams / check 
bunds, tailing dams, construction of buttress walls at toe 
of waste dumps and geo-coir matting for stabilization of 
waste rock dumps.
 • About 96 nos. of wells are being monitored for water 
quality and water levels covering all 4-seasons in a year 
at iron ore projects. Studies are revealed that there has 
been an increasing trend in the ground water level due to 
hydraulic loading by the existing check dams and check 
bunds. Limited usage of ground water and continuous 
recharge helped in the process. One Digital Water Level 
Recorder (video telemetry) and one piezometer are also 
installed at Bailadila Iron Ore Mine, Bacheli Complex for 
regular monitoring of ground water level.
 • NMDC has set-up Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) with 
advanced treatment technology (Sequential Batch 
Reactor) at Bacheli (2 MLD) and Donimalai (3 MLD) 
township for treatment of domestic waste water. STP 
works are in progress at Kirandul (3 MLD) and the treated 
water will be reused for green belt development.
 • About 3 million saplings were planted in and around 
NMDC projects covering an area of 2300 Ha. NMDC 
is also actively contributing funds to Government of 
Chhattisgarh flagship programme “Hariyar Chhattisgarh” 
for undertaking block plantation in the state of C.G by 
CGRVVN Limited. Chhattisgarh Rajya Van Vikas Nigam 
Limited (CGRVVN Ltd). 2 Matri Vans established (1 at 
Bacheli and another at Kirandul) through Chhattisgarh 
Forest Department. 20000 saplings of trees planted 
in above matri vans under the “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” 
program.

CONSERVATION OF ENERGY, TECHNOLOGY ABSORPTION, FOREIGN EXCHANGE EARNINGS AND

About NMDC’s R&D Centre
NMDC’s Research & Development Centre, located at Hyderabad, 
continues to play a pivotal role in advancing mineral processing 
technologies, sustainable iron-making solutions and value addition 
from mining waste. Recognized as a “Centre of Excellence” by the 
United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the 
R&D Centre reflects NMDC’s commitment towards technology-
driven growth, sustainability and national mineral security.
The R&D Centre is equipped with state-of-the-art laboratories and 
pilot-scale facilities covering mineral beneficiation, automated 
mineral analysis, bulk solids flow studies, pelletization and 
agglomeration, analytical characterization, coal and coke-
making studies and extractive metallurgy. Advanced analytical 
infrastructure includes X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Wavelength 
Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (WD-XRF), Inductively Coupled 
Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-AES), Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (SEM), Automatic Mineral Analyser (AMA) 
and other specialized facilities.
The Centre’s NABL-accredited Chemical Laboratory (ISO 
17025:2017) and DSIR recognition continue to strengthen its 
research capabilities and industry credibility. Modernization 
initiatives undertaken at the Patancheru facility during the year 
further enhanced the Centre’s analytical and pilot-scale research 
capacity.
The R&D Centre extends technical support to NMDC’s mining 
and pelletization operations while also serving domestic and 
international public and private sector organizations. Collaborative 
research with premier institutions such as CSIR-IMMT and the 
University of Hyderabad supports innovation in beneficiation, 
waste utilization, circular economy initiatives and sustainable 
mineral processing technologies.
R&D Thrust Areas
A.  Energy Conservation and Sustainability
 • Development of low-energy agglomeration technologies.
 • Dry beneficiation processes for low-grade ores.
 • Waste-to-resource conversion technologies.
 •  Reduction in energy consumption during iron ore 
processing.
 • Improvement in bulk material handling efficiency.B. Technology Integration and Process Automation
 • Advanced mineral characterization and process 
optimization.
 • Implementation of automated analytical and sampling 
systems.
 • Process modelling and pilot-scale validation.
 • Online elemental analysis and process control systems.
Flagship R&D Projects 2025-26:
1. Development of New Products
 Geopolymer Bricks from Mine Waste
 The R&D Centre successfully developed high-strength 
geopolymer bricks utilizing iron ore tailings, overburden 
and mine waste. The cement-free bricks demonstrated 
excellent mechanical properties while significantly reducing 
carbon footprint, supporting sustainable waste-to-resource 
conversion.
 Fused Magnesia from Kimberlite Tailings
 In collaboration with CSIR–IMMT, Bhubaneswar, a laboratory-
scale process was developed for extraction of fused 
magnesia from kimberlite tailings generated from diamond 
mining operations. The project supports import substitution 
and domestic production of magnesium-based refractory 
materials.
2. Process Innovation
 Cold-Bonded Pellet Development
 Alternative binder-based cold-bonded pellets were developed 
to eliminate thermal induration during pellet production. 
Laboratory-scale studies established satisfactory strength 
and reducibility characteristics, indicating potential for 
significant reduction in energy consumption and greenhouse 
gas emissions.
  Dry Beneficiation of Siliceous Blue Dust / Low-Grade Iron Ore
 A two-stage magnetic separation process was developed 
for upgrading high-silica blue dust and low-grade iron ore to 
blast furnace-grade concentrate without use of water. The 
process represents an important step toward sustainable dry 
beneficiation technologies.
 BHQ/BHJ Beneficiation Flowsheet Development
 Deposit-specific beneficiation flowsheets for upgrading BHQ/
BHJ ores into pellet-grade feed material were developed and 
are under further optimization.

Report on Corporate Governance
1.  A brief statement on Company’s 
philosophy on code of Governance
 NMDC Limited, a Navaratna Company, upholds the highest 
standards of governance and ensures transparency, 
accountability and integrity in its operations. Corporate 
governance at NMDC is not just a regulatory requirement but a 
fundamental pillar of our culture, guiding our actions to create 
long-term value for our stakeholders viz. the shareholders, 
customers, suppliers, creditors, Government of India, State 
Governments, Governmental agencies/ departments and the 
society at large.
 The Company’s activities conform to the broader principles 
of financial prudence, customer satisfaction, transparency, 
accountability and commitment to values. NMDC also 
ensures that its policies and practices align with the interest 
of the society at large and the same is demonstrated through 
the Company’s continuous commitment towards stakeholder 
engagement and sustainability.
2. Board of Directors
 As on 31.03.2026, the Board of NMDC comprised of five (5) 
Whole time / Functional Directors including the Chairman & Managing Director, two (2) Government Nominee Directors 
and four (4) Independent Directors. As on 31.03.2026, the 
composition of Board of the Company was as under:-

 During the financial year 2025-26, the Board of the Company 
was duly constituted as per provisions of the Companies Act, 
2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015; except with regard 
to appointment of adequate number of Independent Directors 
including at least one Woman Independent Director. Further, 
as on 31.03.2026, the Board did not have any Woman Director. Being a Government Company and pursuant to Article 74 
of the Articles of Association of the Company, the power to 
appoint Directors on the Board vests with the Administrative 
Ministry viz. Ministry of Steel, Govt. of India. The Company 
has requested the Administrative Ministry from time to time 
for appointment of requisite number of Independent Directors 
on the Board.
 Once the requisite number of Independent Directors (including 
Woman Independent Director) are appointed on the Board, 
the Company will be in compliance of the provisions of 
Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 with 
regard to composition of Board.
 The Chairman & Managing Director and Functional Directors 
are appointed by the Government of India for a period of five 
years or till the age of superannuation or until further orders 
whichever is earlier. The Directors are initially appointed by 
the Board as Additional Directors in terms of the provisions 
of the Companies Act, 2013 and thereafter, the proposal for 
their appointment as Director is put up for approval of the 
shareholders in the General Meeting in terms of provisions of 
Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015.
 In case of Functional Directors, the appointment may be 
terminated by either side on three months’ notice or on 
payment of three months’ salary in lieu thereof. Government 
Nominee Directors representing Ministry of Steel, Government 
of India cease to be Directors from the Board on ceasing 
to be official(s) of Ministry of Steel, Government of India. 
Further, Non-Executive Directors (Independent) are normally 
appointed for a tenure of 3 years by Government of India.
b. BOARD MEETINGS
 Board Meeting Procedure:
 The Board Meetings are convened by giving appropriate 
advance notice after seeking approval of the Chairman 
of the Board / Committee as the case may be. In order to 
address specific urgent needs, meetings are also convened 
at a shorter notice. Resolutions are also passed by way of 
circulation in the eventuality of exigencies or urgency.
 Detailed agenda note are circulated in advance to the Board 
Members for facilitating meaningful, informed and focused 
decision at the meeting. In case of special and exceptional 
circumstances, additional / supplemental agenda item(s) are 
also permitted.

h. Web link of Familiarization Programme:
 In terms of the Articles of Association of the Company, Ministry of Steel, Govt. of India, the Controlling Ministry of the Company 
appoints Independent Directors on the Board of the Company.
 As a process, when a new Independent Director is appointed, a familiarization programme is conducted by the senior management 
team. Further, whenever a new member is appointed to a Board Committee, information relevant to the functioning of the Committee 
and the role and responsibility of Committee members is informed. The Board and Committee meetings of the Company are held 
at least on a quarterly basis and members of the Board meet key functional / business heads separately to get themselves more 
familiarized with the business/ operations and challenges faced by the industry on an ongoing basis.
 Details of the familiarization programmes:
 Programmes organized by Institute of Governance Professional of India and Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs, NMDC Projects 
visits etc.

3. Audit Committee
(a) Brief description of terms of reference
 The role of the Audit Committee shall include the following:-
  Oversight of the Company’s financial reporting process 
and the disclosure of its financial information to ensure 
that the financial statement is correct, sufficient and 
credible;
  Recommendation for appointment, remuneration and 
terms of appointment of auditors of the Company;

www.nmdc.co.in  Approval of payment to statutory auditors for any other 
services rendered by the statutory auditors;
  Reviewing, with the management, the annual financial 
statements and auditor’s report thereon before 
submission to the board for approval, with particular 
reference to:
   Matters required to be included in the Director’s 
Responsibility Statement to be included in the 
Board’s report in terms of clause (c) of sub-section 
3 of section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013;
   Changes, if any, in accounting policies and practices 
and reasons for the same;
   Major accounting entries involving estimates based 
on the exercise of judgment by management;
   Significant adjustments made in the financial 
statements arising out of audit findings;
   Compliance with listing and other legal requirements 
relating to financial statements;
   Disclosure of any related party transactions;
   Modified opinion(s) in the draft audit report.
   Reviewing, with the management, the quarterly financial 
statements before submission to the board for approval;
  Reviewing, with the management, the statement of uses 
/ application of funds raised through an issue (public 
issue, rights issue, preferential issue, etc.), the statement 
of funds utilized for purposes other than those stated 
in the offer document / prospectus / notice and the 
report submitted by the monitoring agency monitoring 
the utilisation of proceeds of a public or rights issue or 
preferential issue or qualified institutional placement  
and making appropriate recommendations to the Board 
to take up steps in this matter;
  Reviewing and monitoring the auditor’s independence 
and performance and effectiveness of audit process;
  Approval or any subsequent modification of transactions 
of the Company with related parties;
  Scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments;
  Valuation of undertakings or assets of the Company, 
wherever it is necessary;  Evaluation of internal financial controls and risk 
management systems;
  Reviewing with the management, the performance of 
statutory and internal auditors and adequacy of the 
internal control systems;
  Reviewing the adequacy of internal audit function, if any, 
including the structure of the internal audit department, 
staffing and seniority of the official heading the 
department, reporting structure coverage and frequency 
of internal audit;
  Discussion with internal auditors of any significant 
findings and follow-up thereon;
  Reviewing the findings of any internal investigations 
by the internal auditors into matters where there is 
suspected fraud or irregularity or a failure of internal 
control systems of a material nature and reporting the 
matter to the Board;
  Discussion with statutory auditors before the audit 
commences about the nature and scope of audit as 
well as post-audit discussion to ascertain any area of 
concern;
  To look into the reasons for substantial defaults in 
the payment to the depositors, debenture holders, 
shareholders (in case of non-payment of declared 
dividends) and creditors;
  To review the functioning of the Whistle Blower 
mechanism;
  Approval of appointment of Chief Financial Officer after 
assessing the qualifications, experience and background, 
etc. of the candidate;
  To review the follow up action on the audit observations 
of the C&AG audit.
  To review the follow up action taken on the 
recommendations of Committee on Public Undertakings 
of the Parliament.
   Provide an open avenue of communication between the 
independent auditor, internal auditor and the Board of 
Directors.
  Review all related party transactions in the Company. 
For this purpose, the Audit Committee may designate a 
member who shall be responsible for reviewing related 
party transactions.

4. Nomination, Remuneration & HR Committee
(a) Brief description of terms of reference:
 The Board of Directors at its 411th meeting held on 24.04.2009 had constituted a Remuneration Committee of Directors in line with 
the DPE OM dated 26.11.2008.
 Subsequently, keeping in view OM No.18(8)/2005-GM dated 14.05.2010 issued by DPE, the Board of Directors at its 430th meeting 
held on 01.02.2011 re-constituted the Remuneration Committee. In compliance with Section 178 of the Companies Act, 2013, 
the Board at its 474th meeting held on 30.05.2014 reconstituted the Remuneration Committee as Nomination & Remuneration 
Committee. The said Committee has been renamed as “Nomination, Remuneration & HR Committee”.
 The scope, powers and terms of reference of the Nomination, Remuneration & HR Committee are as per the directives issued by 
DPE, SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the Companies Act, 2013 etc.

5. Stakeholders Relationship Committee
(a) The Company has in place a Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee headed by an Independent Director to look into various aspects 
of interest of the Stakeholders. The role of the Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee includes the following:
 (1) Resolving the grievances of the security holders including complaints related to transfer/transmission of shares, non-receipt 
of annual report, non-receipt of declared dividends, issue of new/duplicate certificates, general meetings etc.
 (2) Review of measures taken for effective exercise of voting rights by shareholders.
 (3) Review of adherence to the service standards adopted in respect of various services being rendered by the Registrar & Share 
Transfer Agent.
 (4) Review of the various measures and initiatives taken by the Company for reducing the quantum of unclaimed dividends and 
ensuring timely receipt of dividend warrants/annual reports/statutory notices by the shareholders of the Company.

ceiling fixed under the Companies Act, 2013 and as per the guidelines issued by the Government of India. The Company has not 
adopted any mechanism for performance evaluation criteria for Independent Directors.

11. Means of communication
 The Company publishes quarterly Un-audited / Annual Audited financial results through leading National Daily Commercial / 
Economic newspapers and also Local language Daily newspapers including Hindi Daily newspaper, which includes, Financial 
Express, Hindi Milap (Hindi), Vaartha (Telugu), etc. These results are also posted on Company’s website www.nmdc.co.in. The 
Company’s website also contains a dedicated section on ‘Investors’ where shareholders information is available viz. Annual Reports, 
Financial Details, Corporate Investor Presentation, etc.
 In addition, the Company communicates major achievements and important events taking place in the Company through Press, 
Electronic Media - LinkedIn, Facebook, “X”, Instagram and also on its Website. Presentation made to institutional investors / analysts 
are uploaded on Company’s website. Conference call conscripts are also uploaded on the website of the Company.

h. Share Transfer System
 With effect from 01.04.2019, requests for transfer of securities shall be processed only in those cases where the securities are held 
in dematerialized form with a depository, in terms of guidelines issued by SEBI. Further, in terms of SEBI circular dated 25.01.2022, 
while processing investor service requests such as transmission, transposition, renewal, exchange, sub-division, consolidation 
and issue of duplicate certificates etc., the securities shall be issued in dematerialized form only. Accordingly, all shareholders of 
the Company are requested to convert their shareholdings from physical form to demat form at the earliest to reap the benefits of 
dematerialization. Requests for dematerialization of shares are processed and confirmation is given to the respective depositories 
viz, NSDL and CDSL within 15 days.
 SEBI vide Circular dated 03.11.2021, has inter-alia made it mandatory for holders of physical securities to furnish/update PAN, 
email address, mobile number, bank account and nomination details, besides linking their PAN with Aadhar. The said circular also 
prescribes that those folios wherein any one or more of the aforesaid details are not available on or after 30.09.2023 shall be frozen 
and the investor will not be eligible to lodge grievance or avail service request from R&TA and will not be eligible for receipt of 
dividend. In view of the same, members holding shares in physical mode are requested to furnish PAN, KYC details and nomination 
forms immediately to the Company / R&TA in the prescribed forms available on the website of the Company www.nmdc.co.in. 
Special Window for transfer and dematerialization (Demat) of physical shares.
 In accordance with SEBI Circular no. SEBI/HO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026 dated 30.01.2026, special window was 
opened for Transfer and Dematerialization (Demat) of Physical Shares for a period of one year from 05.02.2026 to 04.02.2027 and 
newspaper publication was published in English (Financial Express) and in Telugu (Vaartha) newspapers on 12.05.2026.

Trading
 In pursuance of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) 
Regulations, 2015 and its amendments, the Board of NMDC 
has approved the Internal Code of Conduct for Prevention of 
Insider Trading in dealing with Securities of NMDC Limited. 
The Code is framed with an aim that the employees of the 
Company and his/her Dependents shall not derive any benefit 
or assist others to derive any benefit from the access to and 
possession of Price Sensitive Information about the Company 
which is not in the public domain.

To
The Members of
NMDC Limited
We have examined the compliance of conditions of Corporate 
Governance by NMDC Limited (a Navaratna PSU) (“the Company”), 
for the year ended on March 31, 2026, as per Regulation 15(2) of 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing Regulations’) 
for the period 1st April, 2025 to 31st March, 2026 and the Guidelines 
on Corporate Governance for Central Public Sector Enterprises 
issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), Government 
of India.
The compliance of conditions of Corporate Governance is the 
responsibility of the Management. Our examination was limited 
to review the procedures and implementation thereof, adopted 
by the Company for ensuring the compliance of the conditions of 
Corporate Governance. It is neither an audit nor an expression of 
opinion on the Financial Statements of the Company.
In our opinion and to the best of our information and according 
to the explanations given to us, we certify that, the Company 
has complied with the conditions of Corporate Governance as 
stipulated in the above mentioned Listing Regulations and DPE 
Guidelines, except for:
 As required under Regulation 17(1)(a) & (b) of Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the Company shall have at 
least fifty percent of the Board as Independent Directors, if the 
Chairman of the Company is an Executive Director. However, it 
has been observed that:
 • As on quarter ended 30.06.2025, the Company had 10 
(Ten) Directors including 5 (Five) Executive Directors, 
2 (Two) Nominee Directors and 3 (Three) Independent 
Directors. During the aforesaid period the Company had 
to appoint 4 (Four) more Independent Directors including 
one Woman Independent Director.
 • As on quarter ended 30.09.2025, 31.12.2025 and 
31.03.2026, the Company had 11 (Eleven) Directors 
including 5 (Five) Executive Directors, 2 (Two) Nominee 
Directors and 4 (Four) Independent Directors. During the 
aforesaid period the Company had to appoint 3 (Three) 
more Independent Directors including one Woman 
Independent Director.
 The Company has not filled vacancy in the office of directors 
caused due to expiration of their respective term of office as prescribed under second proviso to Regulation 17 (1E) of 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.
 The constitution of Audit Committee of the Company was not 
as per Regulation 18(1) & (2) of Securities and Exchange Board 
of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 during the period from 01.04.2025 to 
16.05.2025.
 The constitution of Nomination and Remuneration Committee 
of the Company was not as per Regulation 19(1) & (2) of 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 during the 
period from 01.04.2025 to 16.05.2025.
 The constitution of Stakeholders Relationship Committee of 
the Company was not as per Regulation 20(2) of Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 during the period 
from 01.04.2025 to 14.04.2025.
 The constitution of Risk Management Committee of the 
Company was not as per Regulation 21(2) of Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 during the period from 
01.04.2025 to 16.05.2025.
 As required under Regulation 21 (3C) of Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the Company has not 
complied with the requirement of gap of not more than 
two hundred and ten days between two Risk Management 
Committee Meetings.
We further state that such compliance is neither an assurance 
as to the future viability of the Company nor the efficiency or

and efficiency

4. Adoption of low-

5. Deployment of energy 
monitoring systems 
and digital dashboards
6. Integration of climate

cost savings.
3. Proactively managing

NMDC comply 
with environmental 
regulations, avoiding

tires.Positive financial implication:

production reduces 
reliance on raw materials 
and lowers production 
costs.

of waste can reduce 
environmental impact 
and generate additional 
revenue for the company.
3. Strong waste monitoring 
and compliance practices 
help NMDC avoid legal 
fines and financial 
risks tied to regulatory 
violations.

8 Water 
ManagementRisk Mining operations require 
significant volumes of 
water for ore processing, 
beneficiation and dust 
suppression, making 
water management 
a critical operational 
dependency.
NMDC operates in 
regions where water 
availability may be 
constrained and is subject 
to stringent regulatory 
requirements, increasing 
exposure to compliance 
risks. Non-compliance 
with applicable water 
regulations may result 
in legal action, financial 
penalties and reputational 
damage, impacting the 
Company’s license to 
operate.
Additionally, excessive or 
inefficient water use has 
the potential to impact 
local communities and 
surrounding ecosystems, 
leading to stakeholder 
concerns and social risks, 
particularly in water-
stressed areas.
From an operational 
perspective, water 
scarcity or inadequate 
water management 
practices may disrupt 
mining activities, affecting 
production continuity. 
Furthermore, ineffective 
water planning and 
conservation measures 
may reduce the Company’s 
resilience to climate-
related risks, including 
variability in rainfall and 
water availability.1. Conducts regular 
water audits and 
periodic assessments 
of water quality to 
ensure efficient water 
use and compliance 
with environmental 
standards.
2. Processing plants 
feature Zero Liquid 
Discharge at few 
facilities, which 
prevent any liquid 
waste from being 
released into the 
environment,  
thereby minimizing 
water pollution and 
conserving water 
resources.
3 . Wellconstructed  
rainwater harvesting 
structures are 
implemented across 
projects to store 
and reuse rainwater 
for operations, 
reducing dependency 
on external water 
sources.
4. NMDC has established 
Effluent Treatment 
Plants (ETP) and 
Sewage Treatment 
Plants (STP) to treat 
industrial discharge 
and domestic sewage, 
respectively.
5. NMDC has constructed 
a 30lakh cubic meter 
capacity reservoir at 
its processing site in 
Panna to store runoff  
water, meeting the 
demands of NMDC, 
nearby villages and the 
Panna Tiger Reserve.Negative financial 
implication:
1. Noncompliance with 
water management 
regulations, especially in 
waterstressed areas, can 
result in significant fines 
and penalties.
2. Inefficient water 
management can 
potentially lead to 
operational disruptions, 
affecting productivity and 
financial performance. 
Water scarcity or 
mismanagement  
can potentially halt 
operations, leading to 
financial losses due to 
downtime and reduced 
output.
3. Any perceived or 
actual lapses in water 
management can impact 
NMDC’s reputation, 
affecting its social 
license to operate and 
stakeholder trust. This 
can result in decreased 
investor confidence and 
potential loss of business.

2. Does the entity have processes in place to avoid/ manage conflict of interests involving members of the Board? (Yes/No) If Yes, 
provide details of the same.
 Yes, NMDC has processes in place to avoid/ manage conflict of interests involving members of the Board.
 The entity has instituted well-defined policies and governance frameworks to identify, prevent and manage conflicts of interest 
involving members of the Board and Senior Management, in line with SEBI (LODR) Regulations and applicable statutory requirements.
 The Company has a Board-approved Policy on Related Party Transactions (RPTs), which, inter alia, stipulates materiality thresholds 
and lays down a structured process for identification, review and approval of related party transactions. All RPTs are subjected 
to prior review by the Audit Committee, chaired by an Independent Director and are recommended to the Board for approval, as 
applicable.
 Further, a Board-approved Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management requires avoidance of any situation that may 
give rise to an actual or potential conflict of interest with the Company’s interests. All Directors and Senior Management personnel 
provide annual affirmations of compliance with the Code. A consolidated compliance declaration, signed by the Chief Executive 
Officer (CMD), forms part of the Corporate Governance Report.
 Directors are required to periodically disclose their directorships, affiliations and other interests in external entities to the Board. 
In instances where a conflict or potential conflict arises with respect to any agenda item, the concerned Director abstains from 
participation in discussions and decision-making on the matter.

Principle 2: Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is sustainable and safe
Essential indicators
1. Percentage of R&D and capital expenditure (capex) investments in specific technologies to improve the environmental and 
social impacts of product and processes to total R&D and capex investments made by the entity, respectively.
Name of Element FY 2025-26 FY 2024-25 Details of Improvements in environmental and social impacts
Research and 
Development (R&D)3.2% 3.06% NMDC has invested in the development of a microwave-assisted 
hydrogen-based iron ore reduction technology aimed at enabling a low-
carbon ironmaking process. Technology seeks to replace conventional 
carbon-based reductants with hydrogen, thereby reducing carbon dioxide 
emissions associated with iron ore reduction. In addition, microwave-
assisted heating is expected to improve energy efficiency through rapid 
and uniform heat transfer, resulting in optimized process performance 
and lower energy consumption.
The anticipated environmental benefits include reduction in greenhouse 
gas emissions, lower dependence on fossil fuels, improved energy 
efficiency and reduced emissions of conventional air pollutants 
associated with traditional ironmaking routes. The project supports 
cleaner production practices and contributes to NMDC’s efforts towards 
climate change mitigation and sustainable mineral processing
Capex 32.59% 28.80% As part of its sustainability-driven CAPEX strategy, NMDC continues 
to invest in advanced technologies aimed at improving environmental 
and social outcomes across its mining operations. A key initiative in 
this direction is the development of slurry pipeline infrastructure for 
transportation of iron ore fines.
To complement the existing Kirandul–Kothavalasa (K-K) railway system, 
NMDC has adopted slurry pipeline transport from its Bailadila mines. 
This system converts iron ore fines into a concentrated slurry, which is 
transported through pipelines to downstream processing facilities. At 
terminal locations, the slurry is filtered to produce pellet feed concentrate, 
subsequently used in pellet manufacturing for the iron and steel sector.
This CAPEX initiative aligns with global best practices and delivers 
significant sustainability benefits. It minimizes land disturbance through 
underground pipeline infrastructure, reduces dependency on traditional 
logistics and supports lower Scope 3 emissions. The process also enables 
efficient utilization of low-grade fines and slimes, thereby reducing 
mineral wastage and promoting circular resource use. Additionally, the 
pipeline ensures reliable, weather-independent transportation, improving 
operational resilience and enabling accessibility from remote mining 
locations.

3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling and disposing at the end of life, for (a) 
Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste.
 NMDC’s primary product, iron ore, is sold as a raw material to downstream industries where it is transformed into various intermediate 
and finished products, making end-of-life tracking or product reclamation impractical. As a result, NMDC does not operate product 
take-back, reuse, recycling, or end-of-life reclamation programs for the end-of-life of its iron ore as product. The iron ore is used 
to make steel by the downstream industries and the steel scrap is reclaimed and recycled by the industries. However, NMDC has 
established processes for safe handling, recycling and disposal of the waste generated in its operations. These practices ensure 
regulatory compliance and support environmentally responsible operations.

 No.
 EPR is not applicable, as the Company operates in mining of iron ore and does not manufacture products covered under EPR 
regulations.

 Yes.

 b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the 
entity?
  NMDC has established structured processes to identify work -related hazards and assess risks for both routine and non-routine 
activities across its mining operations.
  For routine activities such as drilling, blasting, excavation and material handling, hazard identification and risk assessment are 
carried out through site-specific Safety Management Plans, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Job Safety Analysis 
(JSA). These processes take into account operational and environmental conditions, enabling the identification of hazards and 
implementation of appropriate control measures.
  For non-routine and high-risk activities, including maintenance, shutdowns and emergency interventions, additional controls 
are applied through permit -to-work systems, task -specific risk assessments and supervisory approvals, ensuring risks are 
assessed prior to execution and managed effectively.
  Risk identification and mitigation measures are further supported by periodic review mechanisms. Project audit teams conduct 
internal safety audits twice a year, ensuring a secure work environment by reviewing compliance and following up on audit 
findings. Additionally, all projects undergo quarterly equipment inspections and monitoring, overseen by dedicated teams 
to ensure operational stability and safety. These processes are part of NMDC’s integrated safety management framework, 
supporting systematic identification, assessment and mitigation of occupational health and safety risks.
 c. Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. 
(Y/N)
  Yes.
  NMDC has established processes for workers to report work-related hazards and unsafe conditions through supervisors, shift 
in-charge and site-level reporting mechanisms, where such concerns are formally recorded and addressed.
  The Company’s occupational health and safety framework, aligned with ISO 45001:2018, incorporates Hazard Identification 
and Risk Assessment (HIRA) methodologies and standard safety mechanisms commonly adopted in the mining sector. 
These include permit-to-work (PTW) systems for high-risk and non-routine activities, job safety analysis (JSA), toolbox talks, 
workplace inspections and Lock-out Tag-out (LOTO) procedures to ensure safe isolation of energy sources during maintenance 
and repair activities.
  Workers are encouraged to proactively report unsafe conditions and are empowered to stop work and remove themselves from 
situations posing serious risk to their health and safety until appropriate controls are implemented, without fear of retaliation.
  These processes are supported by periodic safety audits, equipment inspections, safety meetings and supervisory oversight, 
ensuring continuous monitoring and mitigation of occupational health and safety risks.
 d. Do the employees/ worker of the entity have access to non-occupational medical and healthcare services? (Yes/ No)
  Yes.
  NMDC provides access to non-occupational medical and healthcare services to its employees and workers across its operations. 
All major mining projects are supported by on-site hospitals and medical facilities, which cater to both occupational and non-
occupational healthcare needs. These facilities also extend medical support to surrounding communities in nearby villages.

12. Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy workplace.
 NMDC has implemented measures to ensure a safe and healthy workplace across its operations through an occupational health 
and safety framework aligned with statutory requirements and ISO 45001:2018 standards.
 Workplace hazards are identified and managed through Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) and Job Safety Analysis 
(JSA) processes, supported by Standard Operating Procedures and application of the hierarchy of controls. Specific measures are 
implemented to address mining-related risks, including dust control systems and use of personal protective equipment.
 Employee health is supported through Occupational Health Centres at operational sites, which facilitate medical surveillance through 
pre-employment and periodic health check-ups for employees and contract workers. The Company conducts pre-employment 
medical examinations as well as periodic health check-ups for employees and contract workers to monitor occupational and non-
occupational health conditions. OHCs are equipped with diagnostic facilities such as audiometry, X-ray imaging and vision testing 
and medical records are maintained digitally for efficient monitoring and management.
 These measures are supported by regular safety training, audits, inspections and emergency preparedness systems, enabling 
continuous monitoring and improvement of occupational health and safety performance.

1. Provide the processes for consultation between stakeholders and the Board on economic, environmental and social topics or if 
consultation is delegated, how is feedback from such consultations provided to the Board.
 Yes.
 NMDC has established processes for stakeholder consultation on economic, environmental and social topics through stakeholder 
engagement exercises, grievance mechanisms and materiality assessments.
 Stakeholder interactions are primarily conducted at the functional and project levels by relevant departments and site-level 
management, with coordination by the Corporate Sustainability team. Inputs from employees, communities, regulators and other 
stakeholders are captured through these processes.
 The feedback received is consolidated by the respective departments and escalated to senior management. Key issues and material 
topics are reviewed by the CSR and Sustainability Committee and are subsequently presented to the Board for consideration as part 
of strategic oversight, policy formulation and ESG disclosures.
 During FY 2024–25, stakeholder consultations undertaken as part of the materiality assessment were used to identify priority ESG 
topics, which were considered in the Company’s sustainability focus areas and reporting.
2. Whether stakeholder consultation is used to support the identification and management of environmental and social topics (Yes 
/ No). If so, provide details of instances as to how the inputs received from stakeholders on these topics were incorporated into 
policies and activities of the entity.
 Yes.
 Stakeholder consultation is used by NMDC to support the identification and management of environmental and social topics 
through structured engagement processes and periodic materiality assessments involving both internal and external stakeholders.
 During FY 2024–25, stakeholder consultations undertaken as part of the materiality assessment exercise captured inputs from 
employees, communities, regulators and other stakeholder groups. Key concerns identified included environmental management, 
occupational health and safety and community development.
 These inputs were considered in determining priority ESG topics and were reflected in the Company’s focus areas, including 
strengthening environmental management practices, enhancing workplace safety measures and continuing community development 
initiatives in operational areas. The insights also informed updates and alignment of policies related to ESG, environment, human 
rights and occupational health and safety.
 Stakeholder feedback and inputs obtained through Section A Question 25 in this report, is periodically reviewed by management 
and integrated into business strategies, risk management processes and sustainability initiatives, supporting alignment with 
regulatory requirements and stakeholder expectations.

4. Do you have a focal point (Individual/ Committee) responsible for addressing human rights impacts or issues caused or 
contributed to by the business? (Yes/No)
 Yes.
 The Director (Personnel) has overall oversight for human rights matters within the Company. The General Manager (Human 
Resources), designated as the Public Grievance Redressal Officer, serves as the operational focal point for receiving and facilitating 
the resolution of employee and stakeholder grievances, including those relating to human rights, in accordance with the Company’s 
policies and applicable laws.
 Additionally, NMDC also operates under the broader oversight framework of statutory and constitutional bodies such as the National 
Human Rights Commission (NHRC), National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC), National Commission for Scheduled Tribes 
(NCST), National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) and relevant Parliamentary Committees, where applicable and within 
their respective mandates.
5. Describe the internal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.
 NMDC Limited has established structured internal mechanisms to address grievances that may have human rights implications, in 
line with applicable laws, Government of India guidelines and the Company’s internal policies and codes of conduct.
 A formal grievance redressal system is implemented through the Personnel/HR function at the Corporate Office and at Unit/Project 
levels, enabling systematic receipt, review and time-bound resolution of employee concerns.
 The Company’s Vigilance framework, led by the Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO), along with the Board-approved Whistle Blower 
Policy, provides a secure and confidential channel for reporting concerns related to unethical conduct and workplace issues, with 
safeguards against retaliation.
 In addition, statutory and targeted mechanisms are in place, including Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) under the POSH 
Act, 2013, to address sexual harassment cases and designated Liaison Officers for SC/ST employees to address equality-related 
concerns.
 Employees and stakeholders may also access external grievance platforms such as CPGRAMS, which supplement internal 
mechanisms.
 Collectively, these mechanisms support the identification and resolution of grievances with potential human rights implications 
across the Company’s operations.

8. Mechanisms to prevent adverse consequences to the complainant in discrimination and harassment cases.
 NMDC Limited has established mechanisms to prevent adverse consequences to complainants in cases related to discrimination 
and harassment, in line with applicable laws, Government of India guidelines and internal policies.
 The Company operates a Board-approved Whistle Blower Policy, which provides a secure and confidential reporting channel. The 
policy prohibits retaliation or victimization of complainants and ensures protection of identity. In accordance with Department 
of Public Enterprises (DPE) guidelines, the effectiveness of the Whistle Blower Mechanism is periodically reviewed by the Audit 
Committee.
 Complaints received through the Vigilance framework are handled with strict confidentiality and the identity of complainants is 
protected. Where required, administrative safeguards, such as transfer or role reassignment, may be implemented to ensure the 
safety and well-being of complainants and witnesses.
 Statutory and institutional mechanisms further support protection against adverse consequences, including:
 • Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) constituted under the POSH Act, 2013, with defined procedures and safeguards against 
retaliation for women employees;
 • Formal grievance redressal systems across Corporate Office and Unit/Project levels to address workplace concerns in a 
structured and time-bound manner;
 • SC/ST liaison mechanisms, including designated officers, to address concerns related to equality and prevent discrimination.
 Collectively, these mechanisms ensure protection of complainants and enable fair, confidential and effective handling of grievances 
across the Company’s operations.

5. Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage and implementation.
 Certain operations, such as the Kirandul Iron Ore Mine and Donimalai Iron Ore Mine as well as Deposit-  10/11A of the Bacheli Iron 
Ore Mine, primarily employ dry screening processes and therefore do not generate process effluent.
 At the Panna Diamond Mining Project, wet processing is undertaken and water is recycled through tailings storage facilities and 
recirculation arrangements, enabling reuse of water within the process. Accordingly, the project operates under a Zero Liquid 
Discharge framework.
 At applicable operational locations, the Company has implemented water management measures such as water recirculation 
systems, tailings management facilities, Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs) and Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs), in accordance with 
operational requirements and applicable regulatory conditions.

10. Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your 
company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to 
manage such wastes
 NMDC Limited adopts structured waste management practices in line with applicable environmental regulations and Government 
of India guidelines.
 Mining waste primarily comprises overburden and subgrade ore, which are systematically managed through designated waste 
dumps and stockpiles at operational sites. Stabilisation measures such as garland drains, toe walls and geo-coir matting are 
implemented to ensure environmental protection. Low-grade ore is preserved and utilised through blending and beneficiation 
initiatives, supporting resource conservation and reduction in waste generation.
 Process-related waste, including tailings from beneficiation, is managed through tailing dams, with water recovery and reuse 
systems implemented to minimise discharge.
 Hazardous wastes such as used oil, lubricants and contaminated materials are handled in accordance with the Hazardous and 
Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 and are disposed of through authorised recyclers.
 Additional measures include sewage and effluent treatment plants, organic waste converters and biomedical waste management 
facilities at site hospitals, in compliance with applicable regulations.
 These practices collectively support waste minimisation and environmentally sound disposal, while limiting the use and impact of 
hazardous substances in operations.

3. With respect to the ecologically sensitive areas reported at Question 11 of Essential Indicators above, provide details of significant 
direct & indirect impact of the entity on biodiversity in such areas along-with prevention and remediation activities.
 The Panna Diamond Mining Project of NMDC Limited is located in proximity to the Panna Tiger Reserve, within the Gangau Wildlife 
Sanctuary. Mining operations in such areas may have direct impacts, such as land disturbance and habitat modification and indirect 
impacts including dust generation, noise, surface runoff and changes in local hydrology.
 Prevention measures, as specified in Environmental Management Plans (EMP), include controlled blasting techniques to minimise 
vibration and noise, regular monitoring of air, water and noise quality and development of greenbelt areas to reduce dust dispersion. 
Surface water management practices, such as garland drains and check dams, are implemented to control runoff and prevent 
sedimentation in nearby water bodies. Water management practices, including reuse and recycling, are adopted to minimise 
freshwater withdrawal and discharge.
 Additional measures include water conservation initiatives such as development of storage reservoirs at project locations, 
including at the Panna project, which support both operational needs and surrounding ecosystems. Efforts to reduce environmental 
disturbance are also supported through optimised infrastructure usage, including reduced reliance on road-based transportation 
where feasible.
 The project is subject to periodic environmental monitoring and compliance reporting to statutory authorities in line with EC 
conditions. Biodiversity management is further guided by the Company’s Biodiversity Policy, focusing on conservation, impact 
mitigation and responsible environmental management within operational areas.

1 Slurry Pipeline
ProjectNMDC operates six iron ore deposits in the Bailadila Sector 
of Chhattisgarh. To enhance iron ore evacuation, NMDC has 
taken up construction of slurry pipeline from Bailadila to 
Nagarnar at an estimated cost of INR 800 Crore. Currently, 
most iron ore production from Bailadila relies on the KK 
Railway line, which has limitations for transporting over 30 
million metric tons per annum (MPTA). To reduce dependence 
on railways, NMDC adopted an alternative mode of evacuation 
-transporting iron ore fines in slurry form through the Slurry 
Pipeline Project.
This approach also utilizes iron ore slimes by converting them 
into iron ore concentrate. The pipeline is laid underground, 
allowing existing activities to resume after completion. The 
project benefits the local population by creating employment 
opportunities.To reduce the dust and 
particulate emissions during the 
transportation of ore as well as 
reducing scope-3 emissions of 
downstream transportation.

approximately 1.33 million units 
of solar power, contributing 
to reduction in grid electricity 
consumption and associated 
Scope 2 greenhouse gas 
emissions.

5. Does the entity have a business continuity and disaster management plan? Give details in 100 words/ web link.
 NMDC has established comprehensive project-specific Disaster Management Plans (DMPs) as part of its overall risk management 
framework. These plans are aligned with the National Disaster Management Plan, 2019 (NDMP2019), which emphasises prevention, 
mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery measures for disaster resilience.
 NMDC’s plans define roles and responsibilities of designated officials and are supported by regular training, mock drills and periodic 
reviews to ensure operational readiness across sites.

3 Describe the mechanisms to receive and redress grievances of the community.
 NMDC Limited addresses grievances of local communities through established stakeholder engagement practices at its operational 
locations.
 At the project level, community concerns are addressed through interactions with site management and designated officials at 
mining locations. Community issues are typically received and addressed through ongoing engagement with local stakeholders, 
including village representatives and local authorities, as part of routine operational interface.
 As a Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE), NMDC is part of the Government of India’s Centralised Public Grievance Redress and 
Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), which serves as a common grievance redressal platform for all CPSEs. Accordingly, grievances 
received through CPGRAMS are addressed by NMDC as part of its overall grievance redressal framework, in compliance with 
prescribed government timelines and procedures.
 Grievances may also be submitted through formal communication channels, including written representations to project offices or 
the Company’s registered office, which are examined and addressed as per established administrative processes.
 The Company’s approach to community grievance redressal is primarily based on project-level engagement and externally available 
government grievance platforms, ensuring that concerns raised by communities are received and addressed through established 
and compliant mechanisms.
 Link: CPGRAMS-Home

2. Steps taken to inform and educate consumers about safe and responsible usage of products and/or services.
 NMDC Limited operates predominantly in the B2B/B2G segment, supplying iron ore and related products to industrial users such 
as steel manufacturers. Accordingly, direct consumer-facing education on safe usage is not applicable. However, the Company 
supports safe and responsible usage of its products by providing detailed technical specifications, quality parameters and product 
characteristics through its website, contractual documentation and customer interactions. These inputs enable downstream 
industrial users to select appropriate material for their processes and operate within defined quality parameters, thereby supporting 
safe and efficient utilisation. As the products are used as industrial raw materials, responsibility for operational safety in usage 
lies with the downstream users and NMDC’s role is primarily limited to ensuring accurate product information and consistency in 
supply.
3. Mechanisms in place to inform consumers of any risk of disruption/discontinuation of essential services.
 NMDC Limited operates primarily in the B2B/B2G segment as a supplier of iron ore and related bulk raw materials and does not 
provide essential services directly to end consumers. Accordingly, the requirement relating to disruption of essential consumer 
services is of limited applicability.
 However, potential disruptions in supply are communicated to customers through established commercial arrangements and 
operational interfaces. These include provisions within contractual terms, direct communication with customers, notifications 
issued in connection with e-auction processes and updates, where relevant, on the Company’s official website.
 Through these mechanisms, NMDC supports timely communication of relevant information to its customers in line with its 
commercial practices.
4. Does the entity display product information on the product over and above what is mandated as per local laws? (Yes/No/Not 
Applicable) If yes, provide details in brief. Did your entity carry out any survey regarding consumer satisfaction relating to the 
major products / services of the entity, significant locations of operation of the entity or the entity as a whole? (Yes/No)
 Disclosure of Product Information Beyond Statutory Requirements: Yes
 NMDC Limited provides product-related information beyond statutory requirements through its website and product documentation. 
This includes technical specifications such as Fe content, impurity levels (silica, alumina, phosphorus, sulphur) and size gradation 
of products (lumps, fines, pellets). Such information supports customers in understanding product characteristics and usage 
parameters.
